questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Incision should be made in which quadrant of the tympanic membrane so that the chorda tympani is not damaged?
questions.explanation: Myringotomy is conventionally performed in the anteroinferior quadrant of the tympanic membrane. The chorda tympani nerve and ossicles (incus and stapes) lie in the posterosuperior quadrant and are at high risk of trauma if incisions are made superiorly.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Head & Neck - The Ear)
questions.hint: Think about where the ossicles and the chorda tympani traverse (superiorly and posteriorly); safe incision avoids both.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Membranous labyrinth is derived from which embryological structure?
questions.explanation: The membranous labyrinth develops from the otic placode (a thickening of surface ectoderm on either side of the hindbrain) which invaginates to form the otic vesicle (otocyst). The bony labyrinth develops from surrounding mesenchyme (otic capsule).
questions.source: Langman's Medical Embryology, 14th ed., Chapter 19 (Ear)
questions.hint: Recall the surface ectodermal thickening adjacent to the rhombencephalon that invaginates to form the otocyst.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Medial wall of the maxillary sinus contains which structure?
questions.explanation: The medial wall of the maxillary sinus forms the lateral wall of the nasal cavity and contains the maxillary hiatus, which opens into the middle nasal meatus through the lower part of the hiatus semilunaris.
questions.source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed., Chapter 8 (Head and Neck - Nasal Cavity)
questions.hint: The medial wall borders the nasal cavity, communicating directly with one of the meatuses.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Nasal septum injury may damage which structure?
questions.explanation: The nasal septum is primarily composed of the septal (quadrangular) cartilage anteriorly, the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid posterosuperiorly, and the vomer posteroinferiorly. Trauma directly affects these skeletal elements.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11
questions.hint: Identify the key bony and cartilaginous components that form the midline partition of the nose.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Hoarseness of voice results from injury to which nerve?
questions.explanation: The recurrent laryngeal nerve innervates all intrinsic muscles of the larynx except the cricothyroid. Unilateral injury causes paralysis of the ipsilateral vocal cord in the paramedian position, resulting in hoarseness of voice.
questions.source: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy, Vol. 3 (Head & Neck), Chapter 14
questions.hint: Which branch of CN X supplies almost all intrinsic laryngeal muscles controlling vocal fold tension and abduction?

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Locked jaw (inability to open mouth) is due to spasm of which muscle?
questions.explanation: Trismus (lockjaw) is most prominently caused by spasm of the masseter muscle (the powerful mandibular elevator). Masseter spasm locks the jaw shut in conditions like tetanus or temporomandibular joint irritation.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Muscles of Mastication)
questions.hint: This muscle is the primary powerful jaw elevator palpated over the ramus of the mandible.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Child presents with midline neck swelling that moves on swallowing. Which structure is involved?
questions.explanation: A thyroglossal duct cyst is located in or near the midline of the neck (often close to the hyoid bone) and classically moves upward on swallowing and protrusion of the tongue due to its attachment to the base of the tongue via the foramen cecum remnant.
questions.source: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 27th ed., Chapter 48 (The Thyroid Gland)
questions.hint: Notice the midline position and elevation on swallowing, characteristic of embryonic descent of the thyroid gland.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Tonsil present in nasopharynx is the —
questions.explanation: The pharyngeal tonsil (adenoid when enlarged) is situated in the roof and posterior wall of the nasopharynx. Palatine tonsils are in the oropharynx between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Pharynx)
questions.hint: Also known as the adenoids when hypertrophied in children.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.question: Transduction of light into electrical signals occurs in —
questions.explanation: Visual phototransduction is the process by which light is converted into electrical signals in the photoreceptor cells (rods and cones) via rhodopsin/photopsin activation and closing of cGMP-gated cation channels.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 50
questions.hint: Which retinal cells contain the light-absorbing photopigments rhodopsin and iodopsin?

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.question: Transduction of odorants into electrical signals is mediated by —
questions.explanation: Odorant molecules bind to G-protein coupled receptors on the cilia of olfactory sensory neurons (olfactory nerve receptor endings), stimulating adenylate cyclase to generate cAMP and open cyclic nucleotide-gated channels.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 54
questions.hint: Olfactory receptor cells are bipolar neurons whose apical cilia project into the nasal mucus layer.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.question: Chronic kidney disease leading to metabolic alkalosis is due to —
questions.explanation: CKD intrinsically causes metabolic acidosis due to impaired acid excretion and retention of fixed acids (sulfate, phosphate). However, when a patient with CKD paradoxically presents with metabolic alkalosis, it is almost invariably iatrogenic due to excessive loop or thiazide diuretic therapy, which causes volume contraction and hypokalemic alkalosis.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 31; Brenner and Rector's The Kidney
questions.hint: CKD normally causes acidosis; what common therapeutic medication class promotes volume contraction and H+/K+ loss?

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.question: Presbyopia occurs due to —
questions.explanation: Presbyopia is the progressive, age-related loss of accommodation power caused by progressive sclerosis, denaturation of lens proteins, and loss of elasticity of the crystalline lens capsule and matrix.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 50 (The Eye)
questions.hint: As humans age, the lens loses its ability to increase anterior-posterior curvature during accommodation.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.question: Uterine contractility in different stages of labour is mainly controlled by —
questions.explanation: Oxytocin, released in pulses by the posterior pituitary during the Ferguson reflex, directly stimulates forceful, rhythmic myometrial contractions during the active and expulsive phases of labor.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 83
questions.hint: This nonapeptide from the posterior pituitary acts via a positive feedback loop initiated by cervical stretch.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.question: Lactogen produced after delivery is stimulated by the action of —
questions.explanation: Prolactin (from anterior pituitary lactotrophs) is the primary hormone responsible for lactogenesis (milk production and synthesis) in alveolar epithelial cells. (Oxytocin controls milk ejection/letdown).
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 83 (Lactation)
questions.hint: Distinguish milk production/synthesis (prolactin) from milk ejection/letdown (oxytocin).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Insulin directly acts on glycogen synthase by —
questions.explanation: Insulin activates protein phosphatase-1 (PP1) and inhibits glycogen synthase kinase-3 (GSK-3), promoting the dephosphorylated active 'a' form of glycogen synthase, stimulating glycogenesis.
questions.source: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd ed., Chapter 18 (Metabolism of Glycogen)
questions.hint: Insulin generally acts via phosphatases: for glycogen synthase, dephosphorylation triggers activation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Tropic hormones are secreted from —
questions.explanation: Tropic (or trophic) hormones (such as TSH, ACTH, FSH, and LH) are secreted by the anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis) and act by targeting and regulating other peripheral endocrine glands.
questions.source: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd ed., Chapter 41 (The Diversity of the Endocrine System)
questions.hint: Tropic hormones target peripheral glands (thyroid, adrenal cortex, gonads) and originate from the adenohypophysis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Biosynthesis of estriol in ovary occurs through —

options.label: D
options.text: LH stimulation of theca cells alone

questions.explanation: Estriol synthesis relies on the feto-placental unit: fetal adrenal produces DHEA-sulfate, 16α-hydroxylated in fetal liver to 16α-OH-DHEA-S, which is aromatized in the placenta to estriol.
questions.source: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd ed., Chapter 41; Guyton & Hall, 14th ed.
questions.hint: Estriol (E3) requires cooperation between the fetal adrenal, fetal liver, and placenta.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Chemical nature of adrenal medullary hormones is —
questions.explanation: The adrenal medulla synthesizes and secretes catecholamines (epinephrine ~80% and norepinephrine ~20%), derived from the amino acid tyrosine.
questions.source: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd ed., Chapter 41 (Hormones of the Adrenal Medulla)
questions.hint: These hormones are synthesized from tyrosine via L-DOPA and dopamine.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Amino acid present in thyroglobulin for hormone synthesis —
questions.explanation: Thyroglobulin contains specific tyrosine residues that undergo iodination by thyroid peroxidase to form MIT and DIT, which then couple to yield T3 and T4.
questions.source: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd ed., Chapter 41 (Thyroid Hormones)
questions.hint: Iodine is covalently coupled to phenolic rings of which amino acid?

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Demilunes and mucous acini are characteristic of —
questions.explanation: The submandibular gland is a mixed seromucous salivary gland with prominent mucous acini capped by serous demilunes (of Giannuzzi). The parotid gland is purely serous.
questions.source: Wheater's Functional Histology, 6th ed., Chapter 13 (Salivary Glands)
questions.hint: The parotid is purely serous, while this mixed gland displays classic serous demilunes capping mucous units.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: 65-year-old woman with frequent joint pain is most likely due to —
questions.explanation: Postmenopausal decline in estrogen increases osteoclast activity (via RANKL/OPG imbalance), causing rapid trabecular bone loss, fragility, and osteoporotic pain/arthropathy.
questions.source: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed., Chapter 26
questions.hint: Consider the postmenopausal loss of protective gonadal steroid on bone remodeling.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Male with gynecomastia and infertility may have —
questions.explanation: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) is the most common cause of male hypogonadism and primary infertility, presenting with tall stature, testicular dysgenesis, elevated gonadotropins, low testosterone, and gynecomastia.
questions.source: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed., Chapter 7 (Genetic Disorders)
questions.hint: A classic 47,XXY karyotype causing primary testicular failure and elevated LH/FSH with gynecomastia.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Primary function of testosterone —
questions.explanation: Testosterone, secreted by Leydig cells under LH stimulation, drives the development and maintenance of male secondary sexual characteristics and acts with FSH on Sertoli cells to support spermatogenesis.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 81
questions.hint: It is the chief androgen governing male phenotype and sperm maturation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: A person with color blindness (e.g. red-green defect) will have difficulty identifying microscope stains of different colors because —
questions.explanation: Color vision is mediated exclusively by cone photoreceptors in the retina (S-cones, M-cones, L-cones). A mutation or deficiency in the cone opsin photopigments leads to red-green color deficiency.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 50 (Color Vision)
questions.hint: Cones mediate photopic color vision; rods mediate scotopic night vision.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which nerve passes through the foramen rotundum?
questions.explanation: The maxillary nerve (CN V2) passes through the foramen rotundum to enter the pterygopalatine fossa. The mandibular nerve (V3) exits via foramen ovale, and ophthalmic branches pass through the superior orbital fissure.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Cranial Cavity)
questions.hint: Remember the mnemonic: Standing Room Only (Superior orbital fissure = V1, Rotundum = V2, Ovale = V3).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Emissary veins of the scalp are located between which layers of the scalp?
questions.explanation: Emissary veins traverse the loose areolar connective tissue layer (the 4th layer / 'dangerous area' of the scalp) through parietal and mastoid emissary foramina to connect scalp veins with the intracranial dural venous sinuses.
questions.source: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy, Vol. 3, Chapter 2 (Scalp and Face)
questions.hint: Layer 4 (loose areolar tissue) is the 'danger area' of the SCALP because of these valveless connecting veins.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Inability to close eyelids is due to paralysis of which muscle?
questions.explanation: Orbicularis oculi (supplied by the facial nerve, CN VII) is the sole sphincter muscle responsible for closing the palpebral fissure (eyelids). Levator palpebrae superioris (CN III) opens the eyelid.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Face)
questions.hint: The sphincter muscle of the eye innervated by CN VII.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which vein connects the common facial vein to the cavernous sinus?
questions.explanation: The deep facial vein connects the facial vein directly to the pterygoid venous plexus, which communicates with the cavernous sinus through emissary veins (or ophthalmic veins).
questions.source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed., Chapter 8 (Infratemporal Fossa)
questions.hint: This venous communication passes backward from the facial vein across the buccinator to the pterygoid plexus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Hematoma in the infratemporal fossa most likely involves which vessel?
questions.explanation: The maxillary artery is the chief artery running across the lateral pterygoid in the infratemporal fossa. Laceration or trauma here produces a large infratemporal hematoma.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11
questions.hint: The principal terminal branch of the external carotid running through the infratemporal fossa.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A 3-year-old with discharge from the side of the neck, anterior to sternocleidomastoid — defect in which embryonic structure?
questions.explanation: Branchial fistula or sinus results from failure of obliteration of the second pharyngeal cleft (cervical sinus of His), opening along the anterior border of the lower third of the sternocleidomastoid muscle.
questions.source: Langman's Medical Embryology, 14th ed., Chapter 17 (Pharyngeal Apparatus)
questions.hint: The second pharyngeal cleft normally overgrows the 3rd and 4th clefts; persistence leaves an opening along the anterior SCM border.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Pus in the retropharyngeal space lies between which layers of deep cervical fascia?
questions.explanation: The true retropharyngeal space is bounded anteriorly by the buccopharyngeal fascia (covering the pharyngeal constrictors) and posteriorly by the alar layer of the prevertebral fascia.
questions.source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed., Chapter 8 (Deep Cervical Fascia)
questions.hint: Lies between the visceral fascia on the posterior wall of the pharynx and the alar fascia.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Secretomotor fibers to the submandibular gland are carried by —
questions.explanation: Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers from CN VII travel in the chorda tympani, join the lingual nerve (CN V3), synapse in the submandibular ganglion, and postganglionic secretomotor fibers enter the submandibular gland.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11
questions.hint: The chorda tympani 'hitches a ride' on which mandibular branch to reach the ganglion and gland?

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A secretory glandular cell will show abundance of which organelle?
questions.explanation: The PDF marked Mitochondria (vital for ion pumping and ATP synthesis in active transport secretory ducts like striations). Note: protein-secreting serous cells are rich in rough ER/Golgi, but among the provided choices (Mitochondria, Lysosomes, Free ribosomes, Centrioles), Mitochondria is the marked and physiologically active organelle.
questions.source: Wheater's Functional Histology, 6th ed., Chapter 5 (Epithelial Tissues - Glands)
questions.hint: Consider the organelle required to generate high ATP for active secretory transport.
questions.flag_reason: Protein-secreting cells classically have RER/Golgi, but Mitochondria is marked among provided choices.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Difficulty in rotating the neck suggests injury to which nerve?
questions.explanation: The spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) innervates the sternocleidomastoid muscle (which rotates the head to the opposite side) and the trapezius (which elevates the shoulder).
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Cranial Nerves)
questions.hint: Supplies the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Lacrimal sac is located on which wall of the orbit?
questions.explanation: The lacrimal sac lies in the lacrimal groove on the anterior part of the medial orbital wall, formed by the lacrimal bone and the frontal process of the maxilla.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Orbit)
questions.hint: Located in a fossa formed by the lacrimal bone and frontal process of the maxilla on the inner wall.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Lateral wall of the middle ear is formed by —
questions.explanation: The lateral wall of the tympanic cavity is formed largely by the tympanic membrane (and the epitympanic recess bony ring superiorly).
questions.source: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy, Vol. 3, Chapter 15 (Ear)
questions.hint: The eardrum separates the external acoustic meatus from the middle ear cavity.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Defect in neural crest cell signaling affects which ear structure?
questions.explanation: The auditory ossicles derive from pharyngeal arch neural crest: malleus & incus from Arch 1, and stapes head/crura from Arch 2. The stapes footplate originates from the otic capsule (mesodermal), but is frequently tested in NUMS questions as part of ossicular development. Marked B in PDF.
questions.source: Langman's Medical Embryology, 14th ed., Chapter 19
questions.hint: Neural crest cells populate the 1st and 2nd arches to form the ossicles of the middle ear.
questions.flag_reason: Embryologically, stapes footplate is otic capsule derived while head/crura are neural crest 2nd arch; PDF marks footplate of stapes.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Fish bone stuck in throat is most likely lodged in —
questions.explanation: The piriform fossa (recess) is a mucosal depression on each side of the laryngeal inlet where sharp foreign bodies like fish bones commonly lodge, endangering the internal laryngeal nerve beneath the mucosa.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Pharynx)
questions.hint: Deep mucosal recess on either side of the larynx vulnerable to sharp swallowed items.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Taste buds anterior to sulcus limitans are mainly —
questions.explanation: Circumvallate (vallate) papillae (8–12 in number) form a V-shaped line immediately anterior to the sulcus terminalis (limitans) and contain abundant taste buds in their lateral walls.
questions.source: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy, Vol. 3, Chapter 13 (Tongue)
questions.hint: Large dome-shaped papillae arranged in a V-shape right in front of the sulcus terminalis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Superior thyroid artery is a branch of —
questions.explanation: The superior thyroid artery is the first anterior branch of the external carotid artery, arising just below the greater horn of the hyoid bone.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Carotid Arteries)
questions.hint: Arises as the very first branch from the external carotid artery.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Cricothyroid muscle is supplied by —
questions.explanation: The cricothyroid muscle is the sole intrinsic muscle of the larynx innervated by the external laryngeal nerve (a branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, CN X). All other intrinsic laryngeal muscles are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
questions.source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed., Chapter 8 (Larynx)
questions.hint: The single exception to the recurrent laryngeal nerve rule for laryngeal muscles.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Nasolacrimal duct opens into which meatus of the nasal cavity?
questions.explanation: The nasolacrimal duct drains tears from the lacrimal sac into the anterior part of the inferior meatus of the nasal cavity, guarded by Hasner's valve.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Nasal Cavity)
questions.hint: It opens underneath the inferior concha in the lowest meatus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Nerve most commonly injured during thyroidectomy —
questions.explanation: The recurrent laryngeal nerve runs in the tracheoesophageal groove in close intimacy with the inferior thyroid artery, making it the most frequently injured nerve during thyroid surgery.
questions.source: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 27th ed., Chapter 48
questions.hint: Runs close to the inferior thyroid artery near the lower pole and ligament of Berry.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.question: Parathyroid hormone acts through which pathway?
questions.explanation: Parathyroid hormone (PTH) binds to PTH1R, a G-protein coupled receptor (GPCR) that couples to Gs to stimulate adenylate cyclase (increasing cAMP) and Gq to activate PLC/IP3/DAG pathways.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 80
questions.hint: Acts via a membrane receptor that activates Gs/adenylyl cyclase producing intracellular cAMP.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.question: Light reflex absent but accommodation present (Argyll Robertson pupil) — lesion in which area?
questions.explanation: In Argyll Robertson pupil (classically in neurosyphilis), there is bilateral midbrain damage to the pretectal nuclei which mediate the pupillary light reflex, while accommodation fibers bypassing the pretectum to reach Edinger-Westphal are preserved.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 52 (Pupillary Reflexes)
questions.hint: The midbrain relay station specifically required for the pupillary light reflex but spared in accommodation.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.question: Insulin secretion is stimulated by —
questions.explanation: Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) is an incretin hormone secreted by intestinal L-cells that powerfully stimulates glucose-dependent insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 79
questions.hint: An incretin secreted by gut neuroendocrine cells following meal ingestion.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.question: Basement membrane of cornea is called —
questions.explanation: Descemet's membrane is the exceptionally thick, true basement membrane of the posterior corneal endothelium. (Bowman's layer is an acellular condensed anterior stromal layer under the corneal epithelium).
questions.source: Wheater's Functional Histology, 6th ed., Chapter 21 (Special Sense Organs - Eye)
questions.hint: The posterior basement membrane overlying the corneal endothelium.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.question: After exercise, which hormone increases most prominently?
questions.explanation: Strenuous exercise is one of the most potent physiological stimuli for growth hormone (GH) secretion, promoting lipolysis and amino acid uptake into muscles while sparing glucose.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 76
questions.hint: This anterior pituitary anabolic hormone spikes dramatically during and immediately after heavy exercise.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.question: “Umami” taste sensation (e.g., from cheese) is mediated by —
questions.explanation: The umami (savory) taste sensation is elicited predominantly by L-glutamate (monosodium glutamate / MSG) acting on metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluR4) and T1R1+T1R3 heterodimer taste receptors.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 54 (Chemical Senses)
questions.hint: The amino acid responsible for the savory taste of aged cheese, meat broth, and MSG.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.question: X-rays do NOT affect which cells of the testes?
questions.explanation: Leydig (interstitial) cells are non-dividing, radioresistant cells; irradiation causes loss of actively proliferating germ cells (spermatogonia, spermatocytes) causing infertility, but testosterone secretion by Leydig cells remains intact.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 81
questions.hint: These endocrine cells are non-mitotic and therefore relatively resistant to ionizing radiation compared to germ cells.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Enzyme converting norepinephrine to epinephrine —
questions.explanation: Phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase (PNMT), induced by high cortisol levels from the adjacent adrenal cortex, transfers a methyl group from S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) to norepinephrine to synthesize epinephrine.
questions.source: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd ed., Chapter 41
questions.hint: This enzyme requires S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) as the methyl donor and is cortisol-dependent.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are produced by —
questions.explanation: The hepatic cytochrome P450 monooxygenase system frequently leaks electrons directly to molecular oxygen during substrate hydroxylation cycles, generating superoxide and hydrogen peroxide.
questions.source: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd ed., Chapter 12 & 47 (Xenobiotics)
questions.hint: Enzymes in this microsomal heme system leak single electrons to O2 during detoxification.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Central obesity with purple striae suggests —
questions.explanation: Cushing's disease refers specifically to ACTH-hypersecreting pituitary corticotrope adenomas that produce hypercortisolism manifested by truncal obesity, moon facies, buffalo hump, and violaceous abdominal striae.
questions.source: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed., Chapter 24 (Endocrine System)
questions.hint: Cushing *disease* specifically designates pituitary-driven hypercortisolemia.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: High ACTH suppressed only by high-dose dexamethasone indicates —
questions.explanation: In Cushing's disease (pituitary adenoma), ACTH secretion retains partial negative feedback and is suppressed by high-dose dexamethasone (>50% reduction in cortisol). In contrast, ectopic ACTH production (e.g. small cell lung cancer) does not suppress.
questions.source: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd ed., Chapter 41; Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
questions.hint: Pituitary adenomas maintain partial responsiveness to high steroid feedback, whereas ectopic tumors do not.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Increased GH increases IGF levels via —
questions.explanation: GHRH from the hypothalamus stimulates anterior pituitary somatotrophs to synthesize and secrete GH, which in turn acts on hepatocytes to produce and release IGF-1 (somatomedin C).
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 76
questions.hint: The hypothalamic releasing factor directly stimulating growth hormone synthesis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: High ACTH and high cortisol due to —
questions.explanation: Hypothalamic hypersecretion of corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) drives elevated ACTH secretion from the anterior pituitary, which in turn stimulates excessive cortisol secretion from the adrenal cortex.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 78
questions.hint: Excess at the highest hypothalamic level elevates both downstream hormones.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) is raised in —
questions.explanation: Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) is a classic oncofetal glycoprotein tumor marker primarily used for monitoring recurrence and treatment response in colorectal carcinoma.
questions.source: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed., Chapter 7 (Tumor Markers)
questions.hint: The quintessential oncofetal serum marker for colon cancer surveillance.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Increased VEGF leads to —
questions.explanation: Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) is the primary signaling protein promoting new capillary sprout formation and proliferation of endothelial cells (angiogenesis).
questions.source: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed., Chapter 3 (Tissue Repair)
questions.hint: Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor's eponymous biological action.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: According to the Warburg effect, glycolysis predominates in cancer cells leading to —
questions.explanation: The Warburg effect (aerobic glycolysis) provides rapid ATP and glycolytic intermediates needed for macromolecule synthesis in rapidly dividing tumor cells, representing the hallmark 'deregulated cellular energetics'.
questions.source: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed., Chapter 7 (Hallmarks of Cancer)
questions.hint: One of Hanahan and Weinberg's defining hallmarks of cancer involving altered metabolism.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: TP53 mutation in sarcoma or leukemia causes —

options.label: B
options.text: Loss of cell cycle arrest and apoptosis

questions.explanation: p53 acts as the 'guardian of the genome'. Loss-of-function mutations eliminate p21-mediated G1/S cell cycle arrest and prevent BAX-mediated apoptosis following DNA damage.
questions.source: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed., Chapter 7 (TP53)
questions.hint: Normal p53 halts replication at G1 to repair damage or else executes programmed cell death.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Tumor marker CA-125 is elevated in —
questions.explanation: Cancer antigen 125 (CA-125) is a high-molecular-weight glycoprotein elevated in >80% of women with advanced epithelial ovarian carcinoma.
questions.source: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed., Chapter 7 & 22
questions.hint: The standard serological marker for serous surface epithelial tumors of the ovary.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Aging causes —
questions.explanation: Due to the end-replication problem of linear DNA, telomeres progressively shorten with each cell division, eventually triggering replicative cellular senescence (the Hayflick limit).
questions.source: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed., Chapter 1 (Cellular Aging)
questions.hint: Chromosomal ends progressively dwindle with consecutive cell divisions.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: 72-year-old with thick, less pliable skin — cause?

options.label: B
options.text: Cross-linking of collagen by AGEs (advanced glycation end products)

questions.explanation: Non-enzymatic glycation of dermal proteins leads to accumulation of advanced glycation end products (AGEs), which covalently cross-link collagen fibrils, causing skin stiffening and loss of pliability.
questions.source: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd ed., Chapter 47; Robbins 10th ed.
questions.hint: Covalent glucose adducts crosslink extracellular matrix proteins over decades.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: 80-year-old postmortem showing yellow-brown pigment —
questions.explanation: Lipofuscin (the 'wear-and-tear' or aging pigment) is an insoluble yellow-brown granular pigment composed of lipid-protein complexes derived from free-radical peroxidation of subcellular membranes.
questions.source: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed., Chapter 2 (Intracellular Accumulations)
questions.hint: The telltale perinuclear 'wear and tear' pigment in senescent myocardium and hepatocytes.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Chronic alcohol consumption activates which hepatic enzyme?
questions.explanation: Alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) is the primary cytoplasmic enzyme metabolizing ethanol to acetaldehyde. (Note: CYP2E1 is the inducible microsomal system; ADH is the marked option here).
questions.source: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd ed., Chapter 25; Robbins 10th ed.
questions.hint: The major cytoplasmic NAD+-dependent enzyme converting ethanol to acetaldehyde.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Head & Neck (Set 2)
questions.question: Adrenal medulla develops from which germ layer?
questions.explanation: Chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla are derived from migrating neural crest cells (ectodermal origin), functioning as a modified sympathetic ganglion. In contrast, the adrenal cortex derives from coelomic mesoderm.
questions.source: Langman's Medical Embryology, 14th ed., Chapter 16
questions.hint: Think of chromaffin cells as modified postganglionic sympathetic neuroendocrine cells.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Head & Neck (Set 2)
questions.question: Tympanic membrane develops from —
questions.explanation: The tympanic membrane develops from all three germ layers: outer cuticular layer from 1st pharyngeal groove ectoderm, middle fibrous layer from mesenchyme (mesoderm), and inner mucosal layer from 1st pharyngeal pouch endoderm.
questions.source: Langman's Medical Embryology, 14th ed., Chapter 19 (The Ear)
questions.hint: It has an outer skin lining, intermediate fibrous stratum, and inner respiratory mucous lining.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Head & Neck (Set 2)
questions.question: Narrowest part of the laryngeal cavity is —
questions.explanation: In adults, the rima glottidis (the aperture between the true vocal cords and vocal processes of the arytenoid cartilages) is the narrowest part of the laryngeal cavity.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Larynx)
questions.hint: The slit-like aperture between the true vocal folds.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Head & Neck (Set 2)
questions.question: Superior ophthalmic vein drains into —
questions.explanation: The superior ophthalmic vein leaves the orbit through the superior orbital fissure and drains directly into the anterior part of the cavernous sinus.
questions.source: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy, Vol. 3, Chapter 10 (Orbit)
questions.hint: Passes through the superior orbital fissure to enter this large middle cranial fossa sinus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Head & Neck (Set 2)
questions.question: Eyelid drooping (ptosis) with anhidrosis indicates lesion of —
questions.explanation: Horner syndrome is caused by disruption of the cervical sympathetic chain, presenting with the classic triad of partial ptosis (superior tarsal muscle paralysis), miosis (pupillodilator paralysis), and ipsilateral anhidrosis.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Cervical Sympathetic Trunk)
questions.hint: The combination of partial ptosis, pupillary constriction, and facial dryness defines this syndrome.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Head & Neck (Set 2)
questions.question: Hyperacusis with loss of taste indicates facial nerve lesion at —
questions.explanation: DISCREPANCY: The PDF marks A (Stylomastoid foramen). However, the nerve to stapedius (mediating hyperacusis) and chorda tympani (mediating taste) branch proximal to the stylomastoid foramen inside the facial canal. A lesion AT the stylomastoid foramen spares taste and hearing. A lesion at or proximal to the geniculate ganglion / facial canal produces both hyperacusis and loss of taste.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Facial Nerve Lesions); Gray's Anatomy
questions.hint: The branches to stapedius and chorda tympani arise deep inside the facial canal before the exit foramen.
questions.flag_reason: PDF marked A (Stylomastoid foramen), which is anatomically erroneous because hyperacusis & chorda tympani branch within canal; true answer is C (Geniculate ganglion).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Head & Neck (Set 2)
questions.question: Submandibular ganglion and taste fibers from anterior 2/3 tongue are carried by —
questions.explanation: Taste fibers from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and preganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibers (from the chorda tympani) are distributed via the lingual nerve (branch of V3) to the submandibular ganglion.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11
questions.hint: Which branch of the mandibular division carries chorda tympani fibers to the floor of the mouth?

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Head & Neck (Set 2)
questions.question: During parotid gland surgery, which nerve is most likely to be injured?
questions.explanation: The facial nerve (CN VII) enters the posteromedial surface of the parotid gland and divides into its five terminal motor branches (pes anserinus) within the gland parenchyma.
questions.source: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 27th ed., Chapter 46 (Salivary Glands)
questions.hint: The motor nerve that branches within the parotid gland tissue to supply muscles of facial expression.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Head & Neck (Set 2)
questions.question: Artery supplying the external nose primarily is —
questions.explanation: The external nose is primarily supplied by branches of the facial artery (specifically the lateral nasal and superior labial arteries), anastomosing with branches of ophthalmic and maxillary arteries.
questions.source: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy, Vol. 3, Chapter 12 (Nose and Paranasal Sinuses)
questions.hint: The main facial vessel providing lateral nasal and superior labial branches to the dorsum and ala.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Head & Neck (Set 2)
questions.question: Ankyloglossia (tongue-tie) occurs due to —

options.label: A
options.text: Failure of tongue muscles to develop

options.label: B
options.text: Frenulum remaining attached to tongue tip

questions.explanation: Ankyloglossia is an embryological anomaly where the lingual frenulum fails to undergo normal cellular degeneration, remaining short, thick, and attached close to the tip of the tongue.
questions.source: Langman's Medical Embryology, 14th ed., Chapter 17
questions.hint: An abnormally short lingual frenulum tethering the ventral apex of the tongue.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Head & Neck (Set 2)
questions.question: Vertebral artery enters cranial cavity through —
questions.explanation: The vertebral artery ascends through the transverse foramina of C6–C1, pierces the posterior atlanto-occipital membrane, and enters the cranial cavity through the foramen magnum.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11
questions.hint: The largest aperture in the skull base through which the brainstem and vertebral arteries pass.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Head & Neck (Set 2)
questions.question: During thyroidectomy, which structures are at risk of injury?
questions.explanation: Ligation of the superior thyroid artery (near external laryngeal nerve) and inferior thyroid artery (near recurrent laryngeal nerve) are the two key vascular steps posing hemorrhagic and neurovascular risk during thyroidectomy.
questions.source: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 27th ed., Chapter 48
questions.hint: The primary arterial pedicles ligated during removal of thyroid lobes.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Head & Neck (Set 2)
questions.question: A person unable to wrinkle forehead likely has paralysis of —
questions.explanation: The frontalis belly of occipitofrontalis (innervated by the temporal branch of CN VII) raises the eyebrows and wrinkles the skin of the forehead horizontally.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Scalp and Face)
questions.hint: The anterior muscular belly of occipitofrontalis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Head & Neck (Set 2)
questions.question: Superior boundary of the temporal fossa is formed by —
questions.explanation: The temporal fossa is bounded superiorly and posteriorly by the superior and inferior temporal lines, which arch across the frontal and parietal bones.
questions.source: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy, Vol. 3, Chapter 6 (Osteology of Head and Neck)
questions.hint: The arched line on the cranium to which the temporal fascia attaches.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Head & Neck (Set 2)
questions.question: Dangerous space of the neck lies between —
questions.explanation: The 'danger space' of the neck is located between the alar fascia anteriorly and the true prevertebral layer posteriorly. It extends unobstructed from the base of the skull directly into the posterior mediastinum.
questions.source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed., Chapter 8 (Cervical Fascia)
questions.hint: Extends uninterrupted from the skull base down to the posterior mediastinum at the diaphragm.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Head & Neck (Set 2)
questions.question: Cell bodies of photoreceptors (rods and cones) are located in —
questions.explanation: The cell bodies and nuclei of the rod and cone photoreceptors reside in the outer nuclear layer of the retina. (The inner nuclear layer contains nuclei of bipolar, horizontal, and amacrine cells).
questions.source: Wheater's Functional Histology, 6th ed., Chapter 21 (Retina)
questions.hint: The nuclear layer closest to the retinal pigment epithelium.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Head & Neck (Set 2)
questions.question: Epiphora (overflow of tears) results from blockage of —
questions.explanation: Obstruction of the nasolacrimal duct (dacrostenocele / chronic dacryocystitis) blocks the outflow pathway of tears into the inferior meatus, causing tears to spill over the lower eyelid margin (epiphora).
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Lacrimal Apparatus)
questions.hint: The conduit leading from the lacrimal sac into the nasal cavity.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Head & Neck (Set 2)
questions.question: Treacher Collins syndrome results from abnormal development of —
questions.explanation: Treacher Collins syndrome (mandibulofacial dysostosis) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by defective neural crest migration into the first (and second) pharyngeal arches, leading to hypoplastic zygoma and mandible, malformed ears, and eyelid colobomas.
questions.source: Langman's Medical Embryology, 14th ed., Chapter 17 (First Arch Syndrome)
questions.hint: A premier 1st pharyngeal arch dysostosis involving mandibular and zygomatic hypoplasia.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Head & Neck (Set 2)
questions.question: Robin sequence is characterized by —

options.label: B
options.text: Posterior displacement of tongue causing airway obstruction

questions.explanation: Pierre Robin sequence begins with micrognathia (mandibular hypoplasia), which causes glossoptosis (posterior displacement of the tongue), leading to respiratory distress/airway obstruction and a U-shaped cleft palate.
questions.source: Langman's Medical Embryology, 14th ed., Chapter 17
questions.hint: Glossoptosis refers to this backward repositioning of the tongue that obstructs the infant's airway.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Head & Neck (Set 2)
questions.question: CSF rhinorrhea (CSF discharge from nose) occurs due to fracture of —
questions.explanation: Fracture of the delicate, perforated cribriform plate of the ethmoid tears the adherent dura mater and arachnoid, permitting cerebrospinal fluid to leak from the subarachnoid space into the roof of the nasal cavity.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Cranial Cavity)
questions.hint: The fragile, sieve-like horizontal plate in the anterior cranial fossa transmitting CN I fibers.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Head & Neck (Set 2)
questions.question: Fracture involving petrous part of temporal bone and internal acoustic meatus may cause —
questions.explanation: Fractures of the petrous temporal bone frequently lacerate the tympanic membrane and branches of the internal carotid or middle meningeal vessels, causing hemotympanum and active bleeding from the external acoustic meatus (CSF otorrhea/bleeding from the ear).
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11
questions.hint: Trauma through the middle ear and tympanic membrane produces otorrhagia.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Head & Neck (Set 2)
questions.question: The lingual artery runs —
questions.explanation: CRITICAL DISCREPANCY: The PDF marks A ('Over hyoglossus'), but has a handwritten circle around B ('Under hyoglossus') with an arrow pointing to B on page 20! Medically and anatomically, the lingual artery passes DEEP TO (under) the hyoglossus muscle to enter the sublingual region. In contrast, the lingual nerve, deep lingual vein, and hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) pass SUPERFICIAL TO (over) the hyoglossus.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Submandibular Region); BD Chaurasia Vol 3
questions.hint: Hyoglossus separates the superficial lingual nerve and CN XII from the deep lingual artery.
questions.flag_reason: PDF mark A is medically incorrect; handwritten annotation in PDF and anatomy textbooks confirm B (Under hyoglossus).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Head & Neck (Set 2)
questions.question: The upper third of the esophagus is composed of —
questions.explanation: The muscularis externa of the esophagus transitions gradually: upper third is purely striated (skeletal) muscle, middle third is a mixture of striated and smooth muscle, and lower third is purely smooth muscle.
questions.source: Wheater's Functional Histology, 6th ed., Chapter 14 (Gastrointestinal Tract)
questions.hint: Remember the muscular division: top 1/3 skeletal, middle 1/3 mixed, bottom 1/3 smooth.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Bleeding from the tonsillar bed is due to injury of which artery?
questions.explanation: The main arterial supply to the palatine tonsil is the tonsillar branch of the facial artery, which pierces the superior constrictor muscle to enter the lower pole of the tonsillar bed.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Palatine Tonsils)
questions.hint: The primary arterial feeder entering the lower pole from the facial artery.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Facial nerve injury at the stylomastoid foramen causes —

options.label: B
options.text: Paralysis of muscles of facial expression

questions.explanation: At the stylomastoid foramen, only motor fibers to the muscles of facial expression, posterior belly of digastric, and stylohyoid remain. Branches to stapedius and chorda tympani have already left, so taste and hearing are spared.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Facial Nerve Lesions)
questions.hint: Only somatic motor fibers to the face pass through this exit foramen.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Foramen cecum in the tongue represents —
questions.explanation: The foramen cecum of the tongue marks the embryological site of origin of the thyroid diverticulum, which migrates inferiorly along the thyroglossal duct.
questions.source: Langman's Medical Embryology, 14th ed., Chapter 17
questions.hint: The apical pit of the V-shaped sulcus terminalis from which the thyroid gland originates.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Cartilage forming the main portion of the laryngeal inlet —
questions.explanation: The laryngeal inlet (aditus) is bounded anteriorly and superiorly by the upper free border of the epiglottis, laterally by the aryepiglottic folds, and posteriorly by the interarytenoid fold.
questions.source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed., Chapter 8 (Larynx)
questions.hint: The leaf-shaped elastic cartilage guarding the front of the laryngeal aditus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Artery related to the angle of the mandible —
questions.explanation: The facial artery hooks around the inferior border of the mandible at the anteroinferior angle of the masseter muscle (near the angle of the mandible), where its pulsations are easily palpated.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11
questions.hint: Its pulsations are readily felt where it winds around the lower border of the mandible.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Retrusion of the mandible refers to —
questions.explanation: Retrusion (retraction) is the posterior movement of the mandible, accomplished primarily by the horizontal posterior fibers of the temporalis muscle.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (TMJ)
questions.hint: Retraction/retrusion pulls the jaw backward.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Frontalis muscle is supplied by —
questions.explanation: The temporal branch of the facial nerve crosses the zygomatic arch to supply the frontalis belly of occipitofrontalis, corrugator supercilii, and the superior part of orbicularis oculi.
questions.source: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy, Vol. 3, Chapter 2 (Face)
questions.hint: The most superior terminal motor branch crossing over the zygomatic arch.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Muscle responsible for closure of lips —
questions.explanation: The orbicularis oris muscle forms a muscular sphincter surrounding the oral aperture, responsible for closing, pursing, and compressing the lips.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11
questions.hint: The oral sphincter muscle encircling the mouth.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Retraction of tongue is by —
questions.explanation: Styloglossus draws the tongue upward and backward (retraction). (Genioglossus protrudes the tongue; hyoglossus depresses the sides).
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Tongue)
questions.hint: Arises from the styloid process and pulls the tongue posterosuperiorly.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Embryological anomaly characterized by excessive hair growth —
questions.explanation: Hypertrichosis (werewolf syndrome) is an abnormal development and persistence of excess hair follicles resulting from dysregulated epidermal-mesenchymal signaling.
questions.source: Langman's Medical Embryology, 14th ed., Chapter 21 (Integumentary System)
questions.hint: The condition of excess hair growth over normal and abnormal body regions.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Duct of which gland pierces the buccinator muscle?
questions.explanation: The parotid duct (Stensen's duct) crosses the masseter muscle, pierces the buccal fat pad and the buccinator muscle, and opens into the oral vestibule opposite the crown of the upper second molar.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Parotid Gland)
questions.hint: Stensen's duct traverses the buccinator to open inside the cheek.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Roof of the middle ear is formed by —
questions.explanation: The roof (tegmental wall) of the middle ear is formed by the tegmen tympani, a thin plate of the petrous part of the temporal bone separating the tympanic cavity from the middle cranial fossa and temporal lobe.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (The Middle Ear)
questions.hint: A thin plate of petrous bone that separates the middle ear from the middle cranial fossa.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Bilateral cleft lip and jaw arise due to failure of fusion between —
questions.explanation: The PDF marked A ('Medial and lateral nasal processes'). NOTE: In classic embryology, cleft lip results from failure of the maxillary prominence to fuse with the medial nasal prominence (intermaxillary segment). Bilateral cleft lip results when this failure is bilateral. Flagged for review due to question phrasing in local exam keys.
questions.source: Langman's Medical Embryology, 14th ed., Chapter 17 (Cleft Lip and Cleft Palate)
questions.hint: In standard embryology, failure involves maxillary and medial nasal prominences; PDF key marked A.
questions.flag_reason: Embryological standard is maxillary with medial nasal prominence fusion failure; exam key marked A.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Submental triangle primarily drains lymph from —
questions.explanation: The submental lymph nodes (in the submental triangle) drain the tip of the tongue, the central portion of the lower lip, the floor of the anterior mouth, and the mandibular incisors.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Triangles of the Neck)
questions.hint: The apex/tip of the tongue drains bilaterally into this midline submental triangle.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Infection from nasal vestibule can spread to brain via —

options.label: B
options.text: Angular vein → Facial vein → Cavernous sinus

questions.explanation: The nasal vestibule lies in the 'danger area' of the face. Due to valveless facial veins, infection retrogrades via the facial vein and angular vein into ophthalmic veins, reaching the cavernous sinus and causing septic cavernous sinus thrombosis.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Danger Area of the Face)
questions.hint: Retrograde venous flow through the valveless facial-angular-ophthalmic system into the cavernous sinus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: The optic cup is an evagination of —
questions.explanation: The optic vesicles develop as bilateral evaginations from the lateral walls of the forebrain (diencephalon) and invaginate to form the double-walled optic cup.
questions.source: Langman's Medical Embryology, 14th ed., Chapter 20 (The Eye)
questions.hint: The neural retina and optic stalk are direct outgrowths of the diencephalon.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: The papillae without taste buds are —
questions.explanation: Filiform papillae are the most numerous, conical, heavily keratinized papillae covering the anterior two-thirds of the tongue; they provide mechanical friction and contain no taste buds.
questions.source: Wheater's Functional Histology, 6th ed., Chapter 13 (Oral Tissues)
questions.hint: The small, conical, keratinized papillae providing a abrasive surface without gustatory receptors.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Parasympathetic fibers to the otic ganglion are derived from —
questions.explanation: Preganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibers originate in the inferior salivatory nucleus of the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), traverse the tympanic plexus, emerge as the lesser petrosal nerve, and synapse in the otic ganglion.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Otic Ganglion)
questions.hint: Originates from the inferior salivatory nucleus of CN IX via the lesser petrosal nerve.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Thickest component of the cornea —
questions.explanation: The corneal stroma (substantia propria) constitutes approximately 90% of the total corneal thickness and consists of regularly arranged orthogonal collagen lamellae in a glycosaminoglycan ground substance.
questions.source: Wheater's Functional Histology, 6th ed., Chapter 21 (Eye - Cornea)
questions.hint: Constitutes ~90% of the corneal depth, consisting of transparent collagen lamellae.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Diplopia while looking downwards is due to lesion of —
questions.explanation: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) supplies the superior oblique muscle, which depresses the intorted eye. Lesions cause vertical/torsional diplopia that is most severe when reading or walking down stairs (looking down and in).
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Cranial Nerve IV)
questions.hint: Patients typically complain of difficulty reading or walking down stairs.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: General sensation from anterior two-thirds of the tongue is carried by —
questions.explanation: General somatic sensation (pain, temperature, touch) from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is carried by the lingual nerve (a branch of the mandibular nerve, V3). Taste is carried by chorda tympani (CN VII).
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Tongue)
questions.hint: General sensory branch of the mandibular nerve (V3) supplying the anterior oral tongue.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Tensor of the vocal cords is —
questions.explanation: The cricothyroid muscle tilts the thyroid cartilage forward or the cricoid upward, increasing the distance between thyroid and arytenoid cartilages, thereby tensing and elongating the vocal folds.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Larynx)
questions.hint: The sole muscle supplied by the external laryngeal nerve that raises vocal pitch by tensing cords.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Lateral pharyngeal abscess spreads into —
questions.explanation: An infection spreading laterally from the pharynx breaches the superior constrictor into the lateral pharyngeal (parapharyngeal) space, bounded by the pterygoid muscles and carotid sheath.
questions.source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed., Chapter 8 (Fascial Spaces of Neck)
questions.hint: The lateral pharyngeal space is synonymous with this fascial compartment.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Mandibular hypoplasia with external auditory canal defect is a feature of —
questions.explanation: Treacher Collins syndrome (mandibulofacial dysostosis) involves 1st and 2nd branchial arch anomalies, featuring micrognathia, malar hypoplasia, external auditory canal atresia, and conductive deafness.
questions.source: Langman's Medical Embryology, 14th ed., Chapter 17
questions.hint: A 1st and 2nd pharyngeal arch defect affecting mandible, zygoma, and external auditory apparatus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Hormone that reduces metabolic activity at night is secreted by —
questions.explanation: Melatonin is synthesized and secreted rhythmically at night by pinealocytes in the pineal gland under suprachiasmatic nucleus control, regulating circadian sleep-wake cycles and nocturnal metabolic deceleration.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 84 (Pineal Gland)
questions.hint: Secreted in darkness by the pineal gland to modulate circadian rhythm.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Autoimmune destruction of melanocytes leads to —
questions.explanation: Vitiligo is an acquired autoimmune disorder characterized by cell-mediated destruction of epidermal melanocytes, causing sharply demarcated depigmented cutaneous macules and patches.
questions.source: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed., Chapter 25 (Skin)
questions.hint: Autoimmune attack on pigment-producing cells leading to irregular white patches of skin.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Bleeding from deep cervical artery can be controlled by ligating —
questions.explanation: The deep cervical artery is a direct branch of the costocervical trunk (which arises from the second part of the subclavian artery) and ascends in the back of the neck.
questions.source: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy, Vol. 3, Chapter 16 (Subclavian Artery)
questions.hint: The trunk that gives off both the deep cervical artery and the superior intercostal artery.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Tip of the nose is supplied by —
questions.explanation: The tip and ala of the nose are supplied by the external nasal nerve, the terminal cutaneous branch of the anterior ethmoidal nerve (derived from nasociliary nerve, CN V1 ophthalmic division).
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Cutaneous Innervation of Face)
questions.hint: Terminal cutaneous branch of the anterior ethmoidal nerve (CN V1).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: While removing adenoids, numbness of nasopharynx indicates injury to —
questions.explanation: Sensory innervation of the pharynx is predominantly mediated by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) through the pharyngeal plexus (with V2 supplying the anterosuperior nasopharynx). Injury during curettage of adenoids impairs CN IX sensation.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Pharynx)
questions.hint: Provides principal sensory innervation to the pharyngeal mucous membrane.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Anatomy MCQs
questions.question: Chorda tympani incision quadrant (to avoid nerve damage):
questions.explanation: Anteroinferior quadrant of the tympanic membrane is the safest zone for myringotomy because it is furthest from the chorda tympani nerve and ossicular chain situated posterosuperiorly.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11
questions.hint: The safest myringotomy site is situated anteriorly and inferiorly.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Anatomy MCQs
questions.question: Tympanic membrane develops from —
questions.explanation: The tympanic membrane develops from all three germ layers: outer ectoderm of 1st pharyngeal cleft, intervening mesoderm, and inner endoderm of 1st pharyngeal pouch.
questions.source: Langman's Medical Embryology, 14th ed., Chapter 19
questions.hint: It receives contributions from cleft ectoderm, intermediate mesenchyme, and pouch endoderm.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Anatomy MCQs
questions.question: Petrous part of temporal bone fracture with bleeding from ear — structure affected:
questions.explanation: Fractures through the petrous ridge commonly involve the internal acoustic meatus and tegmen tympani, leading to VII/VIII nerve injury, hemotympanum, and bleeding from the ear.
questions.source: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy, Vol. 3, Chapter 15
questions.hint: The bony canal on the posterior surface of the petrous temporal bone carrying VII and VIII.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Anatomy MCQs
questions.question: Bleeding from tonsillar bed is due to injury of —
questions.explanation: The tonsillar branch of the facial artery is the principal arterial supply entering the base/lower pole of the tonsil bed and is the most common cause of primary tonsillectomy arterial bleeding.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11
questions.hint: Branch of the facial artery piercing the superior constrictor muscle.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Anatomy MCQs
questions.question: Facial nerve injury at stylomastoid foramen causes —
questions.explanation: Lesion of CN VII at the stylomastoid foramen spares the chorda tympani, nerve to stapedius, and greater petrosal nerve, producing purely motor facial paralysis (Bell's palsy pattern of ipsilateral facial muscles).
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11
questions.hint: Motor branches to facial expression muscles are knocked out, while taste and stapedius reflexes are spared.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Anatomy MCQs
questions.question: Foramen caecum is related to development of —
questions.explanation: The foramen cecum of the tongue represents the vestigial origin of the median thyroid primordium and thyroglossal duct.
questions.source: Langman's Medical Embryology, 14th ed., Chapter 17
questions.hint: The thyroid diverticulum invaginates from this exact point on the tongue dorsum.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Anatomy MCQs
questions.question: Main cartilage forming the laryngeal inlet —
questions.explanation: The epiglottis forms the superior and anterior boundary of the laryngeal aditus (inlet).
questions.source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed., Chapter 8
questions.hint: The flexible leaf of fibroelastic cartilage closing over the larynx.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Anatomy MCQs
questions.question: Angle of mandible is crossed by —
questions.explanation: The facial artery hooks around the lower border of the mandible just anterior to the angle and masseter muscle insertion.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11
questions.hint: The artery palpated at the lower border of the mandible just in front of masseter.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Anatomy MCQs
questions.question: Muscle responsible for closure of lips —
questions.explanation: The orbicularis oris constitutes the circular sphincter around the oral fissure that closes and presses the lips together.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11
questions.hint: The oral sphincter muscle.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Anatomy MCQs
questions.question: Retraction of tongue is due to —
questions.explanation: The styloglossus muscle arises from the styloid process and pulls the tongue posterosuperiorly (retraction and elevation of margins).
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11
questions.hint: Connects the styloid process to the lateral aspect of the tongue.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Anatomy MCQs
questions.question: Roof of middle ear is formed by —
questions.explanation: The tegmen tympani is a thin lamina of petrous temporal bone that forms the tegmental wall (roof) of the middle ear, separating it from the middle cranial fossa.
questions.source: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy, Vol. 3, Chapter 15
questions.hint: The paper-thin bony plate separating middle ear from temporal lobe.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Anatomy MCQs
questions.question: Tip of nose supplied by —
questions.explanation: The apex and tip of the nose are supplied cutaneously by the external nasal nerve, a branch of the anterior ethmoidal nerve (division of CN V1 ophthalmic).
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11
questions.hint: Branch of the anterior ethmoidal nerve, derived from the 1st division of CN V.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Anatomy MCQs
questions.question: Numbness of nasopharynx during adenoid removal involves which nerve?
questions.explanation: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) provides predominant sensory innervation to the pharyngeal mucosa through the pharyngeal plexus.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11
questions.hint: The ninth cranial nerve mediating pharyngeal sensation and gag reflex afferents.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Anatomy MCQs
questions.question: Diplopia while looking down — nerve involved:
questions.explanation: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) innervates the superior oblique, which depresses the eye in the adducted position. CN IV palsy results in diplopia when looking downwards and medially.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11
questions.hint: Supplies the superior oblique muscle.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Anatomy MCQs
questions.question: Submental triangle drains —
questions.explanation: Lymph from the tip of the tongue, lower lip, and anterior floor of the mouth drains directly to the submental lymph nodes.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11
questions.hint: The anterior tip of the tongue drains into this suprahyoid midline triangle.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Anatomy MCQs
questions.question: Frontalis muscle supplied by —
questions.explanation: The temporal branch of CN VII ascends across the zygomatic arch to innervate the frontalis and upper orbicularis oculi.
questions.source: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy, Vol. 3, Chapter 2
questions.hint: The topmost branch of the facial pes anserinus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Anatomy MCQs
questions.question: Epiphora (tearing) is caused by blockage of —
questions.explanation: Obstruction of the nasolacrimal duct impairs tear drainage into the inferior nasal meatus, resulting in overflow of tears onto the cheek (epiphora).
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11
questions.hint: The duct connecting the lacrimal sac to the nasal cavity.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Anatomy MCQs
questions.question: Treacher Collins syndrome arises from defect in —
questions.explanation: Treacher Collins syndrome is a classic first pharyngeal arch syndrome involving defective neural crest cell migration and proliferation.
questions.source: Langman's Medical Embryology, 14th ed., Chapter 17
questions.hint: Characterized by zygomatic and mandibular hypoplasia derived from Arch 1.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Anatomy MCQs
questions.question: Parotid gland surgery commonly endangers —
questions.explanation: The trunk and branches of CN VII pass through the gland between superficial and deep lobes, putting it at paramount risk during parotidectomy.
questions.source: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 27th ed., Chapter 46
questions.hint: The nerve traversing the parenchyma of the parotid gland.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Anatomy MCQs
questions.question: Lateral pharyngeal abscess spreads to —
questions.explanation: Infection lateral to the pharyngeal wall enters the parapharyngeal (lateral pharyngeal) potential space.
questions.source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed., Chapter 8
questions.hint: The space situated laterally between the pharynx and internal pterygoid muscle.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: Hormone responsible for milk secretion:
questions.explanation: Prolactin acts on breast alveolar epithelial cells to stimulate milk synthesis and secretion into the alveolar lumina.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 83
questions.hint: Anterior pituitary hormone promoting milk production.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: Hormone responsible for milk ejection:
questions.explanation: Oxytocin contracts myoepithelial cells surrounding the breast alveoli, propelling milk from alveoli into the lactiferous ducts (milk let-down/ejection).
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 83
questions.hint: Posterior pituitary hormone contracting myoepithelial cells.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: PTH acts through —
questions.explanation: Parathyroid hormone binds to the PTH1 receptor, stimulating adenylate cyclase via Gs proteins to generate intracellular cAMP.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 80
questions.hint: Acts via Gs-coupled receptor elevating cyclic AMP.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: Light reflex absent but accommodation present due to lesion of —
questions.explanation: Argyll Robertson pupils demonstrate light-near dissociation caused by bilateral lesions in the pretectal area of the midbrain.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 52
questions.hint: The dorsal midbrain nuclei responsible for the afferent limb of the pupillary light reflex.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: After exercise, which hormone increases?
questions.explanation: Exercise is a classic physiologic inducer of growth hormone pulsatile secretion, stimulating lipolysis and muscular protein conservation.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 76
questions.hint: Anterior pituitary hormone that spikes dramatically after intense physical exertion.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: Umami taste (cheese, MSG) due to —
questions.explanation: Umami taste is stimulated by the amino acid glutamate (or MSG), signaling protein-rich foods via metabotropic glutamate receptors.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 54
questions.hint: The amino acid component of monosodium glutamate.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: X-rays do not affect which testicular cells?
questions.explanation: Leydig cells are radioresistant non-dividing endocrine cells; radiation therapy destroys germ cells (azoospermia) while leaving testosterone production largely intact.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 81
questions.hint: The interstitial cells that secrete testosterone.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: Hypothyroidism symptom:
questions.explanation: Hypothyroidism slows the basal metabolic rate, causing anorexia (decreased appetite) alongside weight gain, constipation, cold intolerance, and lethargy.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 77
questions.hint: Reduced appetite (yet accompanied by weight gain due to hypometabolism).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: Lactational amenorrhea is caused by increased —
questions.explanation: High prolactin levels suppress pulsatile GnRH secretion from the hypothalamus, leading to reduced LH and FSH release, preventing ovulation and menstruation during lactation.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 83
questions.hint: Suckling stimulates this hormone, which inhibits hypothalamic GnRH secretion.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: Insulin resistance in pregnancy due to —
questions.explanation: Human placental lactogen (hPL / human chorionic somatomammotropin) exerts anti-insulin and lipolytic actions in the mother, shifting maternal metabolism toward fatty acids and sparing glucose for the fetus.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 83
questions.hint: A placental hormone related to growth hormone that induces gestational maternal insulin resistance.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: Vitamin D deficiency in children causes —
questions.explanation: In growing children before epiphyseal closure, vitamin D deficiency impairs mineralization of growth plates and osteoid, leading to rickets.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 80
questions.hint: Characterized by rachitic rosary, craniotabes, and bowed legs in children.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: Estrogen inhibits osteoclasts by —
questions.explanation: Estrogen upregulates the synthesis of osteoprotegerin (OPG), a decoy receptor that binds RANKL, blocking RANKL-RANK interaction and suppressing osteoclast differentiation and activity.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 80
questions.hint: Increases this soluble decoy receptor that traps RANKL.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: Paget’s disease treatment —
questions.explanation: Calcitonin directly binds to osteoclasts and rapidly inhibits their excessive bone-resorptive activity, functioning as an established therapeutic agent in Paget's disease (alongside bisphosphonates).
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 80
questions.hint: Thyroid parafollicular C-cell hormone that inhibits bone resorption.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: In diabetes insipidus, if ADH increases urine osmolarity — lesion in —
questions.explanation: In central diabetes insipidus (hypothalamic/posterior pituitary defect), exogenous ADH (desmopressin) restores water reabsorption and increases urine osmolarity (>50% increase), confirming that the renal collecting ducts are normal.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 76
questions.hint: A positive response to exogenous vasopressin indicates central (hypothalamic/pituitary) deficiency.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: First stage of labor prolonged due to low —
