questions.explanation: Inadequate oxytocin release or uterine inertia results in hypocontractile uterine activity, leading to prolonged latent or active first stage of labor.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 83
questions.hint: The hormone administered clinically as Pitocin to augment dysfunctional labor.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: Melanin in eye present in —
questions.explanation: Melanin pigment is heavily concentrated in the melanocytes of the iris stroma (determining eye color) and in the posterior pigment epithelium.
questions.source: Wheater's Functional Histology, 6th ed., Chapter 21
questions.hint: Pigment in this stromal structure determines individual eye color.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: Enzyme converting norepinephrine to epinephrine —
questions.explanation: PNMT catalyzes the transfer of a methyl group from SAM to norepinephrine, producing epinephrine in the adrenal medulla.
questions.source: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd ed., Chapter 41
questions.hint: Adrenal medullary enzyme utilizing S-adenosylmethionine to methylate norepinephrine.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) formed by —
questions.explanation: Microsomal oxidation by cytochrome P450 monooxygenases generates ROS through uncoupled catalytic cycles leaking single electrons to O2.
questions.source: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd ed., Chapter 12
questions.hint: Microsomal monooxygenase electron leakage generates ROS during detoxification.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: Superoxide radicals are detoxified by —
questions.explanation: Superoxide dismutase (SOD) specifically converts superoxide anions (O2•–) into hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) and oxygen.
questions.source: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd ed., Chapter 12
questions.hint: Eponymous dismutase converting O2•– into H2O2.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: High ACTH suppressed only by high-dose dexamethasone — diagnosis:
questions.explanation: In Cushing's disease, the pituitary adenoma retains negative feedback sensitivity to supraphysiologic glucocorticoids, showing >50% ACTH/cortisol suppression on high-dose dexamethasone.
questions.source: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd ed., Chapter 41
questions.hint: Suppression on high-dose dexamethasone confirms pituitary etiology.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: Central obesity with purple striae due to —
questions.explanation: Pituitary adenoma (Cushing's disease) overproduces ACTH, causing hypercortisolemia characterized by central adiposity, cutaneous thinning, and purple abdominal striae.
questions.source: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed., Chapter 24
questions.hint: Pituitary source of ACTH causing Cushing's syndrome.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: Increased vascular endothelial growth factor causes —
questions.explanation: VEGF stimulates endothelial cell chemotaxis, proliferation, and capillary vessel sprout formation (angiogenesis).
questions.source: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed., Chapter 3
questions.hint: Growth factor dedicated to creating new blood vessels.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: Warburg effect (glycolysis as main energy in cancer) leads to —
questions.explanation: Aerobic glycolysis in neoplasia provides rapid energy and carbon skeletons for cell growth, representing deregulated cellular energetics.
questions.source: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed., Chapter 7
questions.hint: One of the canonical Hallmarks of Cancer.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: TP53 mutation causes —

options.label: A
options.text: Loss of apoptosis and cell cycle arrest

questions.explanation: Inactivation of TP53 removes the critical checkpoint trigger for p21 cell-cycle arrest and BAX-mediated apoptosis, permitting damaged cells to proliferate.
questions.source: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed., Chapter 7
questions.hint: Disables programmed cell death and G1/S arrest.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: Tumor marker for colorectal cancer —
questions.explanation: Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) is the primary oncofetal marker used to monitor colorectal cancer.
questions.source: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed., Chapter 7
questions.hint: The standard biomarker for colon cancer.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: Tumor marker for ovarian cancer —
questions.explanation: CA-125 is elevated in epithelial ovarian cancers and is used to monitor response to therapy.
questions.source: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed., Chapter 7
questions.hint: Serum marker for epithelial ovarian tumors.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: Aging causes —
questions.explanation: Telomere length decreases with each round of somatic cell division, causing cellular senescence.
questions.source: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed., Chapter 1
questions.hint: Progressive shortening of chromosome end-caps.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: Dry, thickened, less pliable skin in old age due to —

options.label: A
options.text: Collagen cross-linking via advanced glycation end products (AGEs)

questions.explanation: AGEs form cross-links between collagen fibrils in the dermis, decreasing tissue elasticity and skin pliability.
questions.source: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd ed., Chapter 47
questions.hint: Advanced glycation end products crosslink dermal collagen.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: Yellow-brown pigment in elderly postmortem —
questions.explanation: Lipofuscin is the insoluble intracellular aging pigment composed of polymers of lipids and phospholipids complexed with protein.
questions.source: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed., Chapter 2
questions.hint: Wear-and-tear pigment derived from lipid peroxidation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: Alcohol consumption activates —
questions.explanation: Alcohol dehydrogenase in the hepatocyte cytosol oxidizes ethanol to acetaldehyde using NAD+.
questions.source: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd ed., Chapter 25
questions.hint: Cytoplasmic enzyme responsible for primary oxidation of alcohol.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: The lateral boundary of the carotid triangle is formed by which of the following?
questions.explanation: The carotid triangle is bounded posteriorly/laterally by the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, superiorly by the posterior belly of the digastric, and anteroinferiorly by the superior belly of the omohyoid.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Triangles of the Neck)
questions.hint: The large strap-like neck muscle forming the posterior-lateral boundary.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Bleeding from the base of the skull following head injury most commonly occurs due to fracture of:
questions.explanation: Fracture of the delicate cribriform plate of the ethmoid tears meningeal vessels and olfactory nerves, causing anterior fossa hemorrhage and CSF rhinorrhea.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11
questions.hint: The thin, perforated bone in the roof of the nasal cavity.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Food getting stuck between teeth and cheek is due to paralysis of which of the following nerves?
questions.explanation: The buccinator muscle presses the cheek against the teeth and keeps the bolus of food centered on the occlusal surfaces. It is innervated motorically by the buccal branch of the facial nerve (CN VII).
questions.source: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy, Vol. 3, Chapter 2 (Face)
questions.hint: The motor branch of CN VII that supplies the buccinator muscle.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: The outer fibrous layer of the eyeball is formed by:
questions.explanation: The outer protective fibrous coat (tunica fibrosa) of the eyeball consists of the transparent cornea anteriorly (one-sixth) and the opaque white sclera posteriorly (five-sixths).
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Eyeball)
questions.hint: Transparent anterior 1/6th plus opaque posterior 5/6th.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: The lingual artery is a branch of:
questions.explanation: The lingual artery arises as the second anterior branch of the external carotid artery at the level of the greater horn of the hyoid bone.
questions.source: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy, Vol. 3, Chapter 8
questions.hint: Arises from the external carotid opposite the tip of the greater cornu of the hyoid.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Food entering the airway during the second stage of swallowing occurs due to injury of:
questions.explanation: The internal laryngeal nerve provides sensory innervation to the laryngeal mucosa down to the level of the vocal cords. Loss of sensation abolishes the protective cough reflex, allowing food/liquids to enter the larynx silently.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11
questions.hint: Sensory branch of the superior laryngeal nerve guarding the laryngeal inlet.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Somatotrophs in the anterior pituitary are classified as:
questions.explanation: Somatotrophs (producing growth hormone) and lactotrophs (producing prolactin) stain intensely with eosin and are classified histologically as acidophils.
questions.source: Wheater's Functional Histology, 6th ed., Chapter 17 (Endocrine System)
questions.hint: Growth hormone- and prolactin-secreting pituitary cells stain pink with eosin.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: The middle meningeal artery is a branch of which artery?
questions.explanation: The middle meningeal artery is the largest branch of the first (mandibular) part of the maxillary artery, ascending through the foramen spinosum.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11
questions.hint: Arises from the maxillary artery in the infratemporal fossa to enter foramen spinosum.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Conductive deafness occurs due to damage involving structures up to the level of the:
questions.explanation: The conductive hearing apparatus encompasses the external ear and middle ear up to and including the footplate of the stapes in the oval window. Damage to the cochlea or retrocochlear structures causes sensorineural hearing loss.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 53
questions.hint: The innermost ossicle whose footplate contacts the oval window.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: The facial nerve supplies:
questions.explanation: CN VII is the motor nerve of the second branchial arch, innervating all muscles of facial expression, the platysma, stylohyoid, and posterior belly of digastric.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11
questions.hint: The motor nerve derived from the second pharyngeal arch.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: The recurrent laryngeal nerve may be injured during:
questions.explanation: The recurrent laryngeal nerve is in close proximity to the inferior thyroid artery near the inferior pole and ligament of Berry, making thyroidectomy the classic operation endangering this nerve.
questions.source: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 27th ed., Chapter 48
questions.hint: Endocrine neck surgery near the inferior thyroid artery.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: The main source of bleeding during tonsillectomy is:
questions.explanation: The paratonsillar (external palatine) vein descends from the soft palate across the lateral surface of the tonsillar capsule; it is a major and troublesome source of venous hemorrhage during tonsillectomy.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Tonsils)
questions.hint: A large vein descending on the external capsule of the tonsil.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: The artery ligated through the sphenopalatine approach to control posterior epistaxis is:
questions.explanation: Endoscopic surgical ligation of the sphenopalatine artery (ESPAL) as it emerges from the sphenopalatine foramen into the superior/posterior nasal cavity is the gold standard for intractable posterior epistaxis.
questions.source: Scott-Brown's Otorhinolaryngology, 8th ed., Epistaxis; Snell's Anatomy
questions.hint: The terminal branch of the maxillary artery entering the nasal cavity via its eponymous foramen.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: The posterior one-third of tongue develops from which pharyngeal arch?
questions.explanation: The posterior third of the tongue develops from the cranial part of the hypopharyngeal eminence (copula), which is derived mainly from the third pharyngeal arch (explaining its CN IX innervation).
questions.source: Langman's Medical Embryology, 14th ed., Chapter 17 (Tongue Development)
questions.hint: The arch supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: The posterior third of tongue is supplied by which nerve for general and taste sensation?
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) supplies BOTH general sensation and special sensation (taste) to the posterior third of the tongue, including the circumvallate papillae.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Tongue)
questions.hint: Cranial nerve IX carries both gustatory and general sensory fibers for this region.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Eye looking downward and inward is due to paralysis of which muscle?
questions.explanation: The PDF marked 'a) Superior oblique'. Anatomical Note: The physiological primary action of the superior oblique is intorsion and depression in adduction (downward and inward). In trochlear nerve palsy, testing the superior oblique is accomplished by asking the patient to look downward and inward (the field of gaze where weakness causes diplopia). Flagged for review due to question phrasing.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (The Orbit - Extraocular Muscles)
questions.hint: The cardinal gaze position testing the superior oblique is looking downward and inward.
questions.flag_reason: Looking downward and inward is the clinical action / test of SO, but question states 'due to paralysis of'; PDF marks a.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Tip of tongue drains lymph into:
questions.explanation: Lymphatic vessels from the tip of the tongue pass to the submental lymph nodes, which then drain into the deep cervical chain (juguloomohyoid).
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11
questions.hint: The submental nodes lie superficial to the mylohyoid muscle in the midline.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Blowout fracture of the orbit affecting upward gaze is due to damage of:
questions.explanation: Blowout fracture of the thin orbital floor (maxillary bone) causes herniation and entrapment of the inferior rectus muscle and orbital fat, mechanically restricting upward gaze.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Orbit)
questions.hint: Entrapment of this lower orbital muscle prevents the globe from rotating upwards.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Raccoon eyes (bilateral periorbital ecchymosis) occur due to fracture involving:
questions.explanation: Basilar skull fracture involving the anterior cranial fossa (orbital roof of the frontal bone) leads to blood tracking anteriorly into periorbital soft tissues, producing bilateral periorbital ecchymosis ('raccoon eyes').
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11
questions.hint: Anterior cranial fossa / orbital plate fracture.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: The corneal epithelium is:
questions.explanation: The anterior surface of the cornea is lined by a remarkably regular, 5–6 layer thick stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium with exceptional regenerative capacity.
questions.source: Wheater's Functional Histology, 6th ed., Chapter 21
questions.hint: Non-keratinized stratified squamous layer kept moist by tear film.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Lips are red because of:

options.label: a
options.text: Thin epithelium and rich vascular supply

questions.explanation: At the vermilion zone of the lips, the transitional stratified squamous epithelium is thin and translucent, and dermal connective tissue papillae are tall and rich in capillary loops, showing blood color.
questions.source: Wheater's Functional Histology, 6th ed., Chapter 13 (Oral Tissues)
questions.hint: Translucent thin epidermis transmitting the color of rich dermal capillary loops.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Headache above the eyes (involving supraorbital and supratrochlear nerves) indicates infection of:
questions.explanation: The frontal air sinus is innervated by the supraorbital nerve (branch of CN V1), so frontal sinusitis causes referred pain and localized tenderness over the forehead and supraorbital ridge.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Paranasal Sinuses)
questions.hint: Sinus located in the bone of the forehead, innervated by supraorbital branches.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Pain around the medial canthus and bridge of nose is associated with inflammation of:

options.label: a
options.text: Ethmoidal sinus (anterior ethmoidal nerve of V1)

questions.explanation: The anterior and middle ethmoidal air cells are innervated by the anterior ethmoidal nerve; inflammation causes localized pain and tenderness over the medial canthus and nasal dorsum.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11
questions.hint: The sinus group situated in the medial orbital wall.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Submandibular triangle contents include:

options.label: a
options.text: Facial vein, facial artery, hypoglossal nerve, and nerve to mylohyoid

options.label: b
options.text: Internal jugular vein and vagus nerve

questions.explanation: The digastric (submandibular) triangle contains the submandibular gland, facial artery and vein, hypoglossal nerve (CN XII), and the nerve to mylohyoid.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Submandibular Triangle)
questions.hint: Key vessels and nerves crossing superficial and deep to the submandibular gland.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Posterior epistaxis is most commonly due to rupture of:
questions.explanation: Woodruff's plexus and posterior epistaxis in elderly or hypertensive individuals most commonly originate from branches of the sphenopalatine artery.
questions.source: Scott-Brown's Otorhinolaryngology, 8th ed.; Snell's Anatomy
questions.hint: The terminal branch of the maxillary artery supplying the posterior nasal septum and lateral wall.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Anterior nasal septal bleeding (epistaxis) is due to rupture of:
questions.explanation: Kiesselbach's plexus (Little's area) on the anteroinferior septum is the most common site of anterior epistaxis; its prominent anterior contributor is the septal branch of the superior labial artery (from facial artery).
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11
questions.hint: The branch coming up from the upper lip into the anterior nasal septum.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Thyroid gland cells in hyperthyroidism show:
questions.explanation: Active stimulated thyroid follicular cells (e.g. in Graves' disease or under high TSH/TSI stimulation) hypertrophy and become tall columnar, actively absorbing colloid with scalloped margins.
questions.source: Wheater's Functional Histology, 6th ed., Chapter 17 (Thyroid Gland)
questions.hint: Active follicular epithelial cells become tall and columnar, with pale scalloped colloid.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: The submandibular gland has:
questions.explanation: The submandibular gland is a mixed seromucous gland composed predominantly (~80%) of serous acini along with mucous acini and serous demilunes.
questions.source: Wheater's Functional Histology, 6th ed., Chapter 13
questions.hint: Contains both serous and mucous units, but predominantly serous.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: The sublingual gland has:
questions.explanation: The sublingual gland is a mixed tubuloacinar salivary gland with a heavy preponderance of mucous acini.
questions.source: Wheater's Functional Histology, 6th ed., Chapter 13
questions.hint: Predominantly mucous in contrast to the submandibular and parotid glands.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: The parotid gland duct (Stensen’s duct) pierces:
questions.explanation: Stensen's duct crosses the masseter and then pierces the buccinator muscle to open into the oral vestibule opposite the upper 2nd molar tooth.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11
questions.hint: Pierces this cheek muscle to enter the oral cavity.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Tympanic membrane is derived from:

options.label: a
options.text: All three germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm)

questions.explanation: Ectoderm forms the outer cutaneous layer, mesoderm forms the core fibrous stratum, and endoderm forms the inner mucosal lining.
questions.source: Langman's Medical Embryology, 14th ed., Chapter 19
questions.hint: One of the few anatomical structures derived from all 3 germ layers.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: The middle ear cavity communicates with the nasopharynx via:
questions.explanation: The pharyngotympanic (auditory/Eustachian) tube connects the anterior wall of the tympanic cavity with the lateral wall of the nasopharynx, equalizing atmospheric pressure.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11
questions.hint: The conduit equalizing pressure across the tympanic membrane.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Infection from the middle ear can spread to the:
questions.explanation: Suppuration in otitis media can erode the thin tegmen tympani to cause an extradural abscess, meningitis, or temporal lobe abscess in the middle cranial fossa.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Middle Ear Complications)
questions.hint: Erosion through the tegmen tympani leads directly into this cranial fossa.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Back of the scalp is supplied by:
questions.explanation: The greater occipital nerve (medial branch of the dorsal ramus of C2) is the main cutaneous sensory nerve supplying the posterior scalp up to the vertex.
questions.source: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy, Vol. 3, Chapter 2 (Scalp)
questions.hint: Derived from the dorsal ramus of C2 spinal nerve.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Suboccipital triangle contains:
questions.explanation: The suboccipital triangle contains the third part of the vertebral artery lying in its groove on the posterior arch of the atlas, along with the suboccipital nerve (C1 dorsal ramus) and suboccipital venous plexus.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Suboccipital Region)
questions.hint: The third part of this artery lies on the posterior arch of the atlas within the triangle.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Parathyroid glands are located:

options.label: a
options.text: At the poles of the thyroid gland

questions.explanation: The four parathyroid glands lie on the posterior border of the thyroid gland lobes, classically situated near the superior and inferior thyroid poles.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Parathyroid Glands)
questions.hint: Typically found on the posterior capsule near the upper and lower poles of the thyroid lobes.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: The thymus develops from:
questions.explanation: The thymus arises from the ventral portion of the third pharyngeal pouch (alongside the inferior parathyroid glands from its dorsal portion).
questions.source: Langman's Medical Embryology, 14th ed., Chapter 17 (Pharyngeal Pouches)
questions.hint: Shared embryological pouch origin with the inferior parathyroid gland.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: The posterior part of tongue and epiglottis receives sensory supply via:

options.label: a
options.text: Superior laryngeal branch of vagus nerve

questions.explanation: The most posterior part of the tongue (vallecula) and anterior surface of the epiglottis receive both general sensation and taste via the internal laryngeal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (CN X).
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Tongue)
questions.hint: Sensory branch of the vagus nerve innervating the vallecula and epiglottis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Deviation of the uvula to the normal side indicates a lesion of:
questions.explanation: The levator veli palatini muscles are supplied by the vagus nerve (CN X via pharyngeal plexus). Unilateral lesion causes palatal drop on the affected side; upon phonation, the intact contralateral muscle pulls the uvula toward the normal (unaffected) side.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Cranial Nerve X)
questions.hint: The palate fails to elevate on the damaged side, so the uvula points away toward the strong normal side.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Anatomy MCQs
questions.question: Oculomotor nerve palsy causes all except —
questions.explanation: CN III palsy causes complete ptosis (levator palpebrae paralysis), mydriasis (parasympathetic sphincter pupillae paralysis), and a 'down and out' gaze due to unopposed lateral rectus (VI) and superior oblique (IV). Taste sensation is carried by VII, IX, and X, unrelated to CN III.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Cranial Nerve III)
questions.hint: Taste sensation is mediated by cranial nerves VII, IX, and X.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Anatomy MCQs
questions.question: Anterior dislocation of temporomandibular joint is prevented by —
questions.explanation: The lateral temporomandibular ligament reinforces the lateral aspect of the joint capsule and resists excessive posterior and inferior displacement, helping stabilize the mandibular condyle against the articular tubercle.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (TMJ)
questions.hint: The principal intrinsic capsular ligament of the TMJ.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Anatomy MCQs
questions.question: Muscle used to clench the jaw —
questions.explanation: The masseter is the primary powerful muscle of mastication that clenches the teeth firmly together during biting and jaw clenching.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11
questions.hint: Easily palpated over the mandibular ramus when biting down firmly.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Anatomy MCQs
questions.question: Jaw dislocated forward and stuck open — structure preventing this movement?
questions.explanation: In TMJ dislocation, excessive yawning or trauma propels the condylar head forward anterior to the articular eminence. The lateral ligament normally limits excessive movement, but once breached or stretched anteriorly, spasm of masseter and pterygoids locks the jaw open.
questions.source: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy, Vol. 3, Chapter 7 (TMJ)
questions.hint: The main capsular stabilizing ligament of the joint.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Anatomy MCQs
questions.question: One eye with keyhole-shaped iris — defect is called:
questions.explanation: Coloboma iridis is a congenital defect resulting from failure of closure of the choroid (optic) fissure during the 6th–7th week of embryonic development, presenting as a keyhole-shaped defect in the inferior pupillary margin.
questions.source: Langman's Medical Embryology, 14th ed., Chapter 20 (Eye)
questions.hint: Failure of embryonic choroid fissure closure leaving an inferior notch.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Anatomy MCQs
questions.question: Cleft lip results from failure of fusion between —
questions.explanation: Cleft lip arises when the maxillary prominence fails to fuse with the medial nasal prominence (intermaxillary segment) on one or both sides.
questions.source: Langman's Medical Embryology, 14th ed., Chapter 17 (Development of Face)
questions.hint: Fusion between the maxillary prominence and medial nasal prominence is required for normal upper lip formation.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Anatomy MCQs
questions.question: One eye not developed due to failure of formation of —
questions.explanation: Anophthalmia (complete absence of the eye) results from failure of the optic vesicle to evaginate from the diencephalon around the 4th week of gestation.
questions.source: Langman's Medical Embryology, 14th ed., Chapter 20
questions.hint: The earliest outpocketing of the forebrain initiating eye organogenesis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Anatomy MCQs
questions.question: Blow near the angle of mandible affects —
questions.explanation: The masseter muscle inserts directly onto the lateral surface of the mandibular ramus and angle of the mandible, making it directly vulnerable to lateral blunt trauma near the angle.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11
questions.hint: The muscle covering the lateral surface of the ramus and angle.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Anatomy MCQs
questions.question: Asymmetrical smile (drooping corner of mouth) — muscle affected:
questions.explanation: Zygomaticus major (the 'smiling muscle') pulls the angle of the mouth upward and backward. Weakness or paralysis leads to unilateral drooping of the oral commissure.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Facial Muscles)
questions.hint: Known as the muscle of laughing and smiling.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Anatomy MCQs
questions.question: Blow at angle of mandible likely damages —
questions.explanation: The PDF marked A (Medial pterygoid), which inserts into the medial aspect of the mandibular angle. NOTE: On page 48 of the PDF, a handwritten pen line circles C (Masseter), as both Masseter (laterally) and Medial pterygoid (medially) form the pterygomasseteric sling at the angle. Flagged for review.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11
questions.hint: Inserts onto the medial surface of the angle of the mandible opposite the masseter.
questions.flag_reason: PDF marked A (Medial pterygoid) while Masseter is circled in handwritten ink on the PDF page.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Anatomy MCQs
questions.question: Middle meningeal artery passes through —
questions.explanation: The middle meningeal artery ascends from the infratemporal fossa into the middle cranial fossa through the foramen spinosum in the greater wing of the sphenoid.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11
questions.hint: Named for the spine of the sphenoid bone.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Anatomy MCQs
questions.question: Pain near auricular region while chewing (TMJ pain) — ligament strengthened by steroid:
questions.explanation: The lateral temporomandibular ligament supports the capsule and prevents posterior displacement of the neck of the mandible; periarticular or intra-articular steroid injections are directed to relieve capsulitis/ligamentous strain here.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11
questions.hint: The chief intrinsic ligament stabilizing the TMJ capsule.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Anatomy MCQs
questions.question: Parotid duct opens opposite —
questions.explanation: Stensen's duct opens onto a small papilla on the inner surface of the cheek opposite the crown of the second maxillary (upper) molar tooth.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11
questions.hint: Opposite the second upper molar tooth on the oral mucosa.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Anatomy MCQs
questions.question: Retrotonsillar abscess spreads through which muscle?
questions.explanation: The PDF marked A (Palatopharyngeus). Clinically, peritonsillar abscess / retrotonsillar spread involves penetration through the superior constrictor muscle into the parapharyngeal space, though the posterior pillar is formed by palatopharyngeus. Marked A in local key; flagged for review.
questions.source: Scott-Brown's Otorhinolaryngology, 8th ed., Peritonsillar Abscess; Snell's Anatomy
questions.hint: Forms the posterior tonsillar pillar and posterior bed boundary.
questions.flag_reason: Classic anatomical bed is superior constrictor; PDF key marks Palatopharyngeus forming posterior pillar.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Anatomy MCQs
questions.question: Piriform recess closed by —
questions.explanation: Stylopharyngeus descends along the posterolateral pharyngeal wall into the pharynx, blending with the palatopharyngeus and thyroid cartilage near the piriform recess. Marked D in PDF.
questions.source: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy, Vol. 3, Chapter 14 (Pharynx)
questions.hint: Longitudinal pharyngeal muscle passing from the styloid process.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Anatomy MCQs
questions.question: Lateral neck swelling with dysphagia and pain is due to persistence of —
questions.explanation: Persistence of the 2nd pharyngeal cleft forms a branchial cleft cyst (or sinus/fistula) located along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, causing a lateral neck mass with compressive dysphagia.
questions.source: Langman's Medical Embryology, 14th ed., Chapter 17
questions.hint: Second branchial cleft anomalies account for ~95% of lateral branchial anomalies.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Anatomy MCQs
questions.question: Craniofacial defects + thymic & parathyroid aplasia — syndrome:
questions.explanation: DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion) is caused by defective development of the 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouches, resulting in thymic hypoplasia (T-cell immunodeficiency), parathyroid aplasia (hypocalcemic tetany), and conotruncal cardiac defects.
questions.source: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed., Chapter 6 & 7
questions.hint: Classic 22q11 deletion syndrome with hypocalcemia and absent thymic shadow.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Anatomy MCQs
questions.question: Inferior orbital nerve damage causes loss of sensation from —
questions.explanation: The infraorbital nerve (continuation of V2) traverses the orbital floor and exits the infraorbital foramen to supply sensory innervation to the lower eyelid (palpebral branch), lateral nose, and upper lip.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Maxillary Nerve)
questions.hint: Innervates the lower eyelid, cheek, and upper lip.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Anatomy MCQs
questions.question: Infection spread from middle ear to jugular vein via —
questions.explanation: The floor of the middle ear (fundus tympani) is related directly to the superior bulb of the internal jugular vein as it emerges through the jugular foramen; erosion can cause jugular vein thrombophlebitis (Lemierre-type spread).
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11
questions.hint: The foramen through which the sigmoid sinus becomes the internal jugular vein.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.subtitle: Anatomy MCQs
questions.question: Patient unable to wrinkle forehead — muscle affected:
questions.explanation: Frontalis is the muscle responsible for creating horizontal wrinkles on the forehead when elevating the eyebrows.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11
questions.hint: Anterior part of occipitofrontalis.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: 60-year-old with hyperkalemic renal failure treated with insulin + glucose infusion → effect:
questions.explanation: Insulin directly stimulates the activity of the Na+/K+-ATPase in skeletal muscle and hepatic cells, driving extracellular potassium rapidly into the intracellular compartment to temporarily treat dangerous hyperkalemia.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 30
questions.hint: Insulin activates Na+/K+ ATPase, driving potassium intracellularly.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: ADH acts to cause —
questions.explanation: Antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin) binds to V2 receptors in medullary collecting duct principal cells, inserting aquaporin-2 water channels into the apical membrane and promoting free water reabsorption (retention).
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 29
questions.hint: Inserts aquaporin-2 channels in collecting ducts to conserve water.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: In ophthalmoplegia with facial swelling, infection spread via —
questions.explanation: Septic cavernous sinus thrombosis impairs cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2, and VI which run in or along the cavernous sinus walls, producing complete ophthalmoplegia, proptosis, and periorbital/facial edema.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Cavernous Sinus)
questions.hint: The dural venous sinus housing CN III, IV, V1, V2, and VI.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: Stapedius paralysis with hyperacusis — nerve damaged:
questions.explanation: The nerve to stapedius is a motor branch of the facial nerve (CN VII) in the vertical part of the facial canal. Loss of stapedius dampening causes hyperacusis (excessive sensitivity to ordinary sounds).
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 53 (Tympanic Attenuation Reflex)
questions.hint: The stapedius muscle is innervated by a branch of CN VII.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: Sensation bypassing the thalamus and going directly to cortex —
questions.explanation: Olfactory sensory signals bypass the thalamus and project directly from the olfactory bulb/tract to the primary olfactory cortex (piriform cortex, entorhinal cortex, and amygdala).
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 54 (Smell)
questions.hint: The only sensory system whose primary afferents reach cerebral cortex without a mandatory thalamic relay.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: Tremor, tachycardia, sweating, restlessness — likely cause:
questions.explanation: Thyrotoxicosis (hyperthyroidism) markedly upregulates beta-adrenergic receptor expression and sympathetic tone, producing fine tremor, resting tachycardia/palpitations, hyperhidrosis, and agitation.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 77
questions.hint: Hypermetabolic state driven by excessive free T3/T4.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: Test for long-term glycemic control —
questions.explanation: Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) reflects average plasma glucose concentration over the preceding 2–3 months (the ~120-day lifespan of erythrocytes).
questions.source: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd ed., Chapter 47; Guyton & Hall
questions.hint: Measures non-enzymatic glycation of hemoglobin over 8-12 weeks.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: FSH acts on —
questions.explanation: In males, follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) acts specifically on Sertoli 'nurse' cells within the seminiferous tubules, stimulating androgen-binding protein (ABP), inhibin-B, and promoting spermatogenesis.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 81
questions.hint: The testicular nurse cells supporting developing sperm.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: Old man with bilateral hearing loss — cause:
questions.explanation: Presbycusis is age-related bilateral symmetrical high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss resulting from degeneration of hair cells at the basal coil of the cochlea.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 53
questions.hint: Age-related sensorineural hearing impairment.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: Conductive deafness findings in tuning fork tests:

options.label: A
options.text: Rinne negative, Weber lateralized to affected ear

questions.explanation: In pure conductive hearing loss: Bone conduction exceeds air conduction on the affected side (Rinne negative / BC > AC), and Weber test lateralizes to the affected (diseased) ear due to lack of masking ambient background noise.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 53
questions.hint: BC > AC (negative Rinne) and lateralization to the diseased ear on Weber.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: Slow relaxation of ankle jerk seen in —
questions.explanation: Delayed/prolonged relaxation phase of deep tendon reflexes (Woltman's sign of myxedema, classically tested at the Achilles tendon) is pathognomonic of hypothyroidism due to slowed sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium reuptake.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 77
questions.hint: Delayed relaxation phase of the Achilles tendon reflex (Woltman's sign).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: Fetus with intrauterine distress — maternal hormone decreased:
questions.explanation: Maternal serum unconjugated estriol reflects the metabolic integrity of both the fetal adrenal and fetal liver (feto-placental unit). A sharp decline in estriol indicates fetal distress or compromise.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 83
questions.hint: A marker hormone dependent on the fetal adrenal and liver.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: Excessive follicular atresia caused by —
questions.explanation: In conditions like polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), an elevated LH/FSH ratio (high LH with inadequate FSH) drives excessive thecal androgen production and leads to premature follicular arrest and widespread atresia.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 82
questions.hint: The endocrine hallmark of PCOS with an elevated LH-to-FSH ratio.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: Enzyme that breaks H₂O₂ into water and oxygen —
questions.explanation: Catalase, located primarily in peroxisomes, decomposes two molecules of hydrogen peroxide into two molecules of water and one molecule of molecular oxygen (2 H2O2 → 2 H2O + O2).
questions.source: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd ed., Chapter 12 (Biological Oxidation)
questions.hint: Peroxisomal hemoprotein converting 2 H2O2 into water and O2.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: Order of half-lives (longest to shortest):
questions.explanation: hCG has the longest half-life (~24–36 hours) owing to its extensive terminal sialylation on its unique C-terminal peptide, followed by FSH (~3–4 hours) and TSH (~50–60 minutes).
questions.source: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd ed., Chapter 41; Guyton & Hall
questions.hint: Heavily sialylated glycoprotein hormones have markedly delayed hepatic clearance.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: Cortisol secretion occurs in which adrenal zone?
questions.explanation: The zona fasciculata (the thick middle layer of the adrenal cortex) secretes glucocorticoids (cortisol), stimulated by pituitary ACTH.
questions.source: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd ed., Chapter 41 (Adrenal Cortical Hormones)
questions.hint: Mnemonic: GFR = Salt, Sugar, Sex (Fasciculata = Sugar = Cortisol).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: Cytochrome P450 function —
questions.explanation: Cytochrome P450 monooxygenases catalyze Phase I oxidative biotransformation (primarily aliphatic and aromatic hydroxylation) to detoxify xenobiotics and endogenous steroids.
questions.source: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd ed., Chapter 47 (Metabolism of Xenobiotics)
questions.hint: The primary Phase I microsomal hydroxylation system.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: Lipid component present in cytochrome P450 —
questions.explanation: Phosphatidylcholine is the essential phospholipid required to reconstitute active cytochrome P450 reductase and cytochrome P450 in endoplasmic reticulum microsomal membranes.
questions.source: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd ed., Chapter 47
questions.hint: The major neutral membrane phospholipid (lecithin) essential for CYP450 activity.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: Hyperkalemia treated with insulin + glucose — mechanism:
questions.explanation: Insulin stimulates the Na+/K+-ATPase in cell membranes, stimulating potassium influx into skeletal muscle cells and lowering serum potassium.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 30
questions.hint: Shifts extracellular potassium ions into intracellular stores.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: Which is not a free radical?
questions.explanation: Hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) is a reactive oxygen species (ROS), but it does not have an unpaired electron in its outer valence shell; therefore, by definition, it is not a free radical (unlike OH•, O2•–, and NO•).
questions.source: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd ed., Chapter 12; Robbins Pathology 10th ed.
questions.hint: A non-radical reactive oxygen species lacking an unpaired electron.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: Insulin promotes which enzymatic action?
questions.explanation: Insulin induces transcription of glucokinase in liver and pancreatic beta cells, promoting glucose phosphorylation and trapping during hyperglycemia. Gluconeogenic enzymes (PEPCK, Pyruvate carboxylase) are repressed.
questions.source: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd ed., Chapter 17 (Glycolysis & Oxidation of Pyruvate)
questions.hint: Induces the high-Km liver hexokinase isoform.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A boxer is hit on the side of his head and becomes unconscious. CT scan shows an epidural hematoma. Which bony feature is most likely fractured?
questions.explanation: The pterion is an H-shaped sutural junction in the temporal fossa overlying the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery. Fractures here lacerate the artery, causing an acute epidural (extradural) hematoma.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (The Pterion)
questions.hint: The H-shaped junction of frontal, parietal, sphenoid, and temporal bones.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A patient presents after a head injury with hemotympanum, facial nerve palsy, and hearing loss. CT shows a fracture passing through the petrous part of the temporal bone. Which nerve is most likely damaged?
questions.explanation: The facial nerve (CN VII) and vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII) travel through the internal acoustic meatus and petrous temporal bone. Petrous bone fractures frequently injure the facial nerve within the fallopian canal, producing peripheral facial palsy.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Facial Nerve)
questions.hint: Cranial nerve VII traversing the facial canal within the petrous temporal bone.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A patient undergoing hair transplant surgery experiences unexpected heavy bleeding from the anterior scalp. Which artery is most likely injured?
questions.explanation: The anterior scalp is supplied by the supratrochlear and supraorbital arteries (terminal branches of the ophthalmic artery). Incisions over the frontal anterior scalp can lacerate the supratrochlear artery.
questions.source: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy, Vol. 3, Chapter 2 (Scalp)
questions.hint: A branch of the ophthalmic artery exiting the superomedial orbital margin.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A 63-year-old man undergoes parotid gland surgery. Postoperatively, he cannot close his right eye and has drooping of the mouth corner. Which structure was likely damaged during surgery?
questions.explanation: The main trunk and branching plexus of the facial nerve (CN VII) divide within the parenchyma of the parotid gland into temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, and cervical branches.
questions.source: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 27th ed., Chapter 46
questions.hint: The motor nerve to the face embedded within the substance of the parotid gland.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A 19-year-old patient presents with a swollen and tender submandibular lymph node. Which of the following regions is most likely the source of infection?

options.label: B
options.text: Lateral side of face and eyelids

questions.explanation: Submandibular nodes receive efferent lymphatics from the submental nodes (draining central lower lip and chin) and directly drain the lateral parts of the lower lip, cheek, and anterior nasal cavity.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Lymphatic Drainage of Head & Neck)
questions.hint: Efferent lymphatic drainage from the submental basin passes to the submandibular nodes.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A newborn is diagnosed with Treacher Collins syndrome, characterized by mandibular hypoplasia, downward slanting palpebral fissures, and malformed ears. This condition is due to abnormal development of structures derived from which pharyngeal arch?
questions.explanation: Treacher Collins syndrome results from defective migration and survival of neural crest cells into the first pharyngeal arch (mandibular arch).
questions.source: Langman's Medical Embryology, 14th ed., Chapter 17 (First Arch Syndrome)
questions.hint: The mandibular arch giving rise to the lower jaw and zygoma.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: During surgical removal of a tumor in the infratemporal fossa, the surgeon accidentally injures a large arterial branch of the external carotid artery. Profuse bleeding occurs. Which artery is most likely involved?
questions.explanation: The maxillary artery is the primary large arterial trunk running directly through the infratemporal fossa across the lateral pterygoid muscle.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Infratemporal Fossa)
questions.hint: The principal artery traversing the infratemporal fossa.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A 32-year-old female presents with painless enlargement of lymph nodes in the anterior triangle of the neck. Which group of lymph nodes is primarily involved?
questions.explanation: The deep cervical lymph node chain forms a vertical collar along the internal jugular vein deep to the sternocleidomastoid in the anterior/lateral cervical region and is the final common lymphatic pathway for the head and neck.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11
questions.hint: The primary deep chain running along the internal jugular vein.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A 50-year-old man presents with a rapidly enlarging, painless swelling in the left supraclavicular region. Biopsy reveals metastatic cancer. This lymph node is commonly referred to as Virchow’s node. Which primary cancer site is most likely?
questions.explanation: Virchow's node (Troisier's sign) is an enlarged left supraclavicular node that receives metastatic spread via the thoracic duct classically from gastric adenocarcinoma (stomach cancer).
questions.source: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed., Chapter 17 (Gastric Cancer)
questions.hint: Classic abdominal adenocarcinoma metastasis via the thoracic duct.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A 45-year-old woman with thyroid cancer undergoes a neck dissection. The surgeon identifies and ligates the middle thyroid vein, which drains into which of the following structures?
questions.explanation: The middle thyroid vein is a short, wide vein that emerges from the lateral border of the thyroid gland, crosses the common carotid artery, and empties directly into the internal jugular vein.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Thyroid Gland)
questions.hint: Drains directly laterally into the deep great vein of the neck.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A 34-year-old patient has horizontal diplopia and cannot abduct the left eye. This suggests a lesion of the abducent nerve (CN VI). Where is the most likely site of compression?
questions.explanation: The abducent nerve (CN VI) runs freely through the lumen of the cavernous sinus immediately lateral to the internal carotid artery, making it exceptionally susceptible to cavernous sinus thrombosis or aneurysmal compression.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Cavernous Sinus)
questions.hint: The abducens nerve runs directly inside the center of this dural venous sinus beside the internal carotid.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A patient with trauma to the orbit is unable to elevate the affected eye when looking medially, but other eye movements are intact. Which muscle and nerve are affected?
questions.explanation: The inferior oblique muscle (innervated by CN III) is the primary elevator of the eye when the globe is in the fully adducted (medial) position.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Extraocular Muscles)
questions.hint: In adduction, the visual axis aligns with the line of pull of this oblique muscle to produce pure elevation.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A patient complains of pain and swelling in the floor of the mouth, especially during meals. On examination, a stone is palpated in the Wharton’s duct. Which gland is most likely involved?
questions.explanation: Wharton's duct is the excretory duct of the submandibular gland. Sialolithiasis most frequently affects this duct (~80%) due to viscous, alkaline saliva ascending against gravity.
questions.source: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 27th ed., Chapter 46
questions.hint: Wharton's duct drains this salivary gland.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A histology slide of a salivary gland shows purely serous acini, intercalated and striated ducts, and prominent connective tissue septa. Which of the following best describes the function of this gland?

options.label: C
options.text: Serous secretion rich in amylase and ions

questions.explanation: The parotid gland is a purely serous exocrine gland containing zymogen granules that secrete watery saliva rich in alpha-amylase (ptyalin), proline-rich proteins, and electrolytes.
questions.source: Wheater's Functional Histology, 6th ed., Chapter 13 (Parotid Gland)
questions.hint: The purely serous parotid gland produces watery secretion packed with alpha-amylase.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A patient with blunt trauma to the eye complains of loss of peripheral vision. Examination reveals detachment of the retina. Which layer is separated in retinal detachment?
questions.explanation: In rhegmatogenous or traumatic retinal detachment, fluid accumulates in the potential space between the outer retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and the inner neural neurosensory retina (derived from the optic cup layers).
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Retina)
questions.hint: Separation occurs between the neurosensory retina and the underlying pigmented epithelial monolayer.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A patient complains of central vision loss but intact peripheral vision. Fundoscopy shows degeneration of the central part of the retina. Which structure is most likely affected?
questions.explanation: Age-related macular degeneration or foveal pathology selectively compromises the fovea centralis (the macula lutea center with the highest cone density), causing loss of high-acuity central vision while preserving peripheral vision.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 50
questions.hint: The retinal depression responsible for maximum visual acuity and central sight.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A child presents with night blindness. Vitamin A deficiency is suspected. Which retinal layer or cell type is primarily affected?
questions.explanation: Vitamin A (11-cis-retinal) is a required prosthetic group for rhodopsin in rod photoreceptors. Depletion impairs rhodopsin regeneration, leading to nyctalopia (night blindness).
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 50 (Photochemistry of Vision)
questions.hint: The photoreceptor cells mediating vision in dim/scotopic illumination.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A patient complains of dizziness and loss of balance. Clinical tests suggest a problem with the vestibular system. Which structure of the inner ear is primarily responsible for sensing angular acceleration?
questions.explanation: The cristae ampullares within the ampullae of the three semicircular ducts sense rotational and angular acceleration of the head.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 56
questions.hint: The three orthogonal fluid-filled ducts detecting head rotation.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A child is born with conductive hearing loss and malformed ossicles. The condition is linked to faulty development of the ear ossicles. These ossicles originate from which embryological structure?
questions.explanation: The auditory ossicles develop from the cartilages of the pharyngeal arches: malleus and incus from Meckel's cartilage (Arch 1) and stapes from Reichert's cartilage (Arch 2).
questions.source: Langman's Medical Embryology, 14th ed., Chapter 19
questions.hint: Meckel's and Reichert's cartilages of the first and second branchial arches.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: During a dental procedure, a patient experiences numbness of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. Which nerve is most likely affected?
questions.explanation: The lingual nerve lies in close proximity to the lingual cortical plate of the mandibular 3rd molar. Inferior alveolar nerve blocks or wisdom tooth extractions can injure it, producing numbness of the anterior 2/3 of the tongue.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Lingual Nerve)
questions.hint: Branch of V3 running immediately lingual to the mandibular third molar.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A patient complains of difficulty in speech and food manipulation. On examination, there is deviation of the tongue to the right upon protrusion. Which muscle is most likely affected?
questions.explanation: Genioglossus is the primary tongue protruder. When the right CN XII or right genioglossus is paralyzed, the intact left genioglossus pushes the tongue toward the paralyzed (right) side.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Tongue Muscles)
questions.hint: The 'safety muscle' of the tongue responsible for protrusion.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A 2-day-old infant has difficulty swallowing and exhibits an abnormally large tongue protruding from the mouth. This condition is commonly associated with which of the following?
questions.explanation: Congenital macroglossia refers to an abnormally enlarged tongue (seen in Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, congenital hypothyroidism, or Down syndrome), causing feeding and respiratory difficulty.
questions.source: Langman's Medical Embryology, 14th ed., Chapter 17
questions.hint: Pathological enlargement of the tongue.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A 35-year-old man complains of loss of taste sensation from the anterior part of his tongue. Histologically, which type of papillae is primarily responsible for this function?
questions.explanation: Fungiform papillae are mushroom-shaped, vascular papillae scattered across the tip and dorsolateral margins of the anterior tongue that contain apical taste buds innervated by the chorda tympani.
questions.source: Wheater's Functional Histology, 6th ed., Chapter 13
questions.hint: Mushroom-shaped papillae containing taste buds across the anterior tongue.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A 50-year-old man presents with frontal headache that worsens when he leans forward. Imaging shows fluid in the frontal sinus. Through which structure does the frontal sinus drain into the nasal cavity?
questions.explanation: The frontal sinus drains through the frontonasal duct into the ethmoidal infundibulum, which opens into the anterior part of the hiatus semilunaris in the middle meatus.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Paranasal Sinuses)
questions.hint: The crescent-shaped groove in the middle meatus into which the frontonasal duct empties.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A patient presents with hoarseness following thyroid surgery. Laryngoscopy reveals immobility of one vocal cord. Which nerve was most likely injured during the procedure?

options.label: A
options.text: External branch of superior laryngeal nerve

questions.explanation: Unilateral injury to the recurrent laryngeal nerve during thyroid surgery causes ipsilateral vocal cord paralysis (in paramedian position), manifesting as vocal hoarseness and weak phonation.
questions.source: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 27th ed., Chapter 48
questions.hint: Branch of the vagus nerve closely related to the inferior thyroid artery.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A 7-year-old child develops periorbital swelling and pain following an upper respiratory tract infection. Imaging reveals infection spreading from a paranasal sinus into the orbit. Which sinus is most likely involved?
questions.explanation: The paper-thin lamina papyracea of the ethmoid bone forms the medial wall of the orbit. Ethmoid sinusitis in young children easily breaches this boundary, causing orbital cellulitis.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Orbit)
questions.hint: Separated from the orbit only by the paper-thin lamina papyracea.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A 55-year-old female presents with neck swelling and hoarseness of voice. Examination shows an enlarged thyroid gland. Which structure is likely being compressed due to its close anatomical relation to the thyroid?
questions.explanation: An invasive or massively enlarged thyroid mass compresses the recurrent laryngeal nerve in the tracheoesophageal groove, causing vocal fold paresis and hoarseness.
questions.source: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 27th ed., Chapter 48
questions.hint: Runs in the tracheoesophageal groove immediately posterior to the thyroid lobes.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A 38-year-old woman has episodes of headache, palpitations, and sweating. Imaging reveals a tumor in the adrenal medulla. What condition is most likely responsible for her symptoms?
questions.explanation: Pheochromocytoma is a catecholamine-secreting tumor of chromaffin cells in the adrenal medulla presenting with the classic episodic triad of headaches, palpitations, and diaphoresis (sweating).
questions.source: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed., Chapter 24 (Adrenal Medulla)
questions.hint: Chromaffin cell tumor causing paroxysmal surges of catecholamines.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: Which of the following stated mechanisms correspond with attenuation reflex?

options.label: a
options.text: It can increase the intensity of low frequency sound transmission by 30-40 decibels

options.label: b
options.text: It increases the rigidity of ossicle system, thereby reducing conduction of low frequency sound.

options.label: c
options.text: It occurs following a latent period of 4-8 seconds after a loud sound

options.label: d
options.text: It protects cochlea from the damaging vibration of relatively quiet but high frequency sounds

questions.explanation: The tympanic attenuation reflex (contraction of stapedius and tensor tympani) increases the rigidity of the middle ear ossicular chain, attenuating transmission of loud, low-frequency sounds (<1000 Hz) by 30 to 40 decibels to protect the cochlea.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 53 (Tympanic Membrane and Ossicular System)
questions.hint: Contraction of stapedius and tensor tympani stiffens the ossicular chain.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: Which of the following substances elicits the sensation of bitter taste?
questions.explanation: Bitter taste is triggered by organic nitrogenous bases and plant alkaloids (such as quinine, strychnine, and nicotine) acting via T2R G-protein coupled receptors.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 54 (Primary Sensations of Taste)
questions.hint: Nitrogenous plant bases like quinine and nicotine.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: Which of the following statements describe the role of basilar membrane correctly?

options.label: a
options.text: It contains basilar fibers whose diameter increases from the base of cochlea to the apex of cochlea.

options.label: b
options.text: It contains basilar fibers whose length decreases from the base of the cochlea to the apex of cochlea.

options.label: c
options.text: It separates the scala media from the scala vestibuli.

options.label: d
options.text: It vibrates best at high frequency near the base of cochlea, whereas it vibrates best at low frequency at the apex of the cochlea.

questions.explanation: MULTIPLE MARKS IN PDF: The PDF shows green checkmarks on BOTH (a) and (d). Statement (d) is the quintessential tonotopic physiological principle (Bekesy traveling wave theory): high frequency waves peak at the stiff, short base, while low frequencies travel to the compliant, wide apex (helicotrema). Statement (a) is also marked in the PDF key.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 53 (Frequency Resonance on the Basilar Membrane)
questions.hint: Tonotopic organization dictates high-frequency resonance at the stiff base and low-frequency at the wide apex.
questions.flag_reason: Multiple marks in PDF: Both options a and d have green ticks. Option d is the core physiological concept.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: What is the name of the condition in which lens of the eye becomes almost totally unaccommodating in person older than 70 years?
questions.explanation: Presbyopia is the physiological age-related decline in accommodative amplitude. By approximately 70 years of age, accommodative power is practically zero (loss of lens elasticity).
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 50 (Optics of the Eye)
questions.hint: Age-related loss of lens accommodation.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: Which one of the following conditions is caused by the lesion of optic chiasma?
questions.explanation: The optic chiasm contains decussating nasal hemiretinal fibers carrying visual input from both temporal visual fields. Compression (e.g. pituitary adenoma) produces bitemporal heteronymous hemianopia.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 52 (Visual Pathways)
questions.hint: Pituitary mass compressing crossing nasal fibers produces tunnel vision.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: Which one of the following statements corresponds correctly with astigmatism?

options.label: a
options.text: Light rays being emitted from distant objects are focused behind the retina

options.label: b
options.text: Light rays being emitted from distant objects are focused in front of retina

options.label: c
options.text: Light rays being emitted from distant objects are in sharp focus on the retina

options.label: d
options.text: There is an opaque or cloudy area in lens

questions.explanation: The PDF marked 'a'. NOTE: Medically, focusing behind the retina defines hyperopia, while astigmatism is unequal curvature along different refractive meridians of the cornea. In local examination question banks, questions occasionally contain overlapping definitions; marked 'a' in the PDF key.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 50
questions.hint: Focusing behind retina corresponds to hyperopia, but is the marked key in this exam.
questions.flag_reason: Definitional discrepancy: astigmatism is non-spherical curvature, whereas option a defines hyperopia.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: Olfactory receptor cells belong to which of the following group of cells?
questions.explanation: Olfactory receptor cells are genuine primary bipolar neurons located in the olfactory neuroepithelium, with an apical dendrite extending cilia into mucus and a basal unmyelinated axon traversing the cribriform plate.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 54
questions.hint: Primary sensory neurons possessing two poles (dendrite and axon).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: Which of the following events causes rods to hyperpolarize in response to light?

options.label: a
options.text: Decrease in sodium conductance into the outer segment

options.label: b
options.text: Decrease in sodium pump activity at the inner segment

options.label: c
options.text: Increase in potassium conductance into the outer segment

options.label: d
options.text: Increase in sodium conductance into the outer segment

questions.explanation: Light activates transducin and phosphodiesterase (PDE6), hydrolyzing cGMP to 5'-GMP. Closure of cGMP-gated Na+ channels halts the 'dark current' of inward sodium flux, causing hyperpolarization (-40 mV to -70 mV).
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 50 (Phototransduction)
questions.hint: Light causes closure of cGMP-dependent sodium channels in the outer segment.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: The actions of GH are mediated in part by which of the following?
questions.explanation: Many growth-promoting anabolic actions of growth hormone (such as epiphyseal cartilage proliferation and bone elongation) are mediated indirectly through hepatic secretion of somatomedins (principally IGF-1).
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 76
questions.hint: Also known as Insulin-like Growth Factors (IGFs).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: A 45-year-old woman has a cerebrovascular accident that causes necrosis of the posterior pituitary. Which of the following effects is most likely to be seen?
questions.explanation: Loss of posterior pituitary ADH secretion causes central diabetes insipidus. Unrestricted renal free-water excretion causes intense polyuria; if water intake cannot match loss, dehydration results in severe hypernatremia.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 29 & 76
questions.hint: Diabetes insipidus leads to excessive water loss, concentrating serum sodium.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: GH acts on which of the following cells to cause long bone growth?
questions.explanation: GH and IGF-1 act directly on epiphyseal plate chondrocytes, stimulating their replication and differentiation to expand cartilage columns, which undergo subsequent endochondral ossification.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 76
questions.hint: Cartilage-forming cells in the epiphyseal growth plates.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: Growth hormone secretion would be suppressed by the following condition:
questions.explanation: MULTIPLE MARKS IN PDF: Both (a) Somatostatin (growth hormone-inhibiting hormone) and (b) Acute hyperglycemia physiologically suppress GH secretion. The PDF has green checkmarks on BOTH 'a' and 'b'. Deep sleep and exercise stimulate GH secretion.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 76
questions.hint: Both somatostatin and elevated blood glucose act as potent suppressors of GH.
questions.flag_reason: Multiple correct answers: Both Somatostatin and Acute hyperglycemia carry green checkmarks in the PDF.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: Dwarfism differs from cretinism in that:
questions.explanation: The PDF marked 'b) There is stunted height'. Clinically, both cretinism (congenital hypothyroidism) and pituitary dwarfism exhibit stunted height; the classic distinguishing hallmark is that cretinism features severe mental retardation and coarse facies, whereas pituitary dwarfism has normal proportionate cognitive intellect. Flagged for review.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 76 & 77
questions.hint: Both have stunted height, but cretinism uniquely causes severe mental retardation; PDF marked b.
questions.flag_reason: Both conditions feature stunted growth; cretinism has mental retardation. Marked b in PDF.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: Blood level of which of the following substances is decreased in Graves' disease?
questions.explanation: In Graves' disease, thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI) autonomously activate the TSH receptor, causing high circulating T3/T4. Negative feedback at the anterior pituitary suppresses pituitary TSH secretion to undetectable (<0.01 mIU/L) levels.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 77
questions.hint: High free thyroid hormones exert strong negative feedback on pituitary thyrotrophs.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: Which of the following functions inhibits the secretion of growth hormone by the anterior pituitary?
questions.explanation: Hypothalamic somatostatin binds to somatostatin receptor subtype 2 (SSTR2) on somatotrophs, inhibiting adenylyl cyclase via Gi and suppressing growth hormone release.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 76
questions.hint: Also designated as Growth Hormone-Inhibiting Hormone (GHIH).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: A 46-year-old man has "puffy" skin and is lethargic. His plasma thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration is low and increases markedly when he is given thyrotropin-releasing hormone. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: a
options.text: Hyperthyroidism due to a thyroid tumor

options.label: b
options.text: Hyperthyroidism due to an abnormality in the hypothalamus

options.label: c
options.text: Hypothyroidism due to an abnormality in the hypothalamus

options.label: d
options.text: Hypothyroidism due to an abnormality in the pituitary

options.label: e
options.text: Hypothyroidism due to an abnormality in the thyroid

questions.explanation: CRITICAL DISCREPANCY: The PDF marks (d) 'Hypothyroidism due to an abnormality in the pituitary'. However, if exogenous TRH administration produces a marked rise in TSH, the pituitary thyrotrophs are fully intact and functional! The defect is lack of endogenous TRH secretion by the HYPOTHALAMUS (tertiary hypothyroidism, option c). If pituitary pathology existed, TSH would fail to respond to TRH. Flagged for review.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 77; Harrison's Endocrinology
questions.hint: A vigorous TSH rise following TRH proves the pituitary is intact, pointing the lesion to the hypothalamus.
questions.flag_reason: Physiological discrepancy: If TSH rises upon TRH, pituitary works and hypothalamus is defective (c), but PDF marked d.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: Which of the following hormones is both synthesized and stored in the pituitary gland?
questions.explanation: Growth hormone is synthesized and stored within secretory granules in anterior pituitary somatotrophs. Vasopressin is synthesized in the hypothalamus and only stored in posterior pituitary terminals.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 76
questions.hint: An anterior pituitary peptide synthesized de novo by somatotrophs.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
