questions.question: In controlling aldosterone secretion, angiotensin II acts on which of the following structures?
questions.explanation: Angiotensin II binds to AT1 receptors on cells of the zona glomerulosa (the outermost zone of the adrenal cortex), activating phospholipase C to stimulate aldosterone synthase and aldosterone secretion.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 78
questions.hint: The outermost mineralocorticoid-producing zone of the adrenal cortex.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: The cause of involution of corpus luteum is

options.label: b
options.text: High levels of FSH from anterior pituitary

options.label: c
options.text: High levels of HCG in blood

options.label: d
options.text: Low levels of Estrogen and Progesterone

questions.explanation: In non-pregnant cycles, luteolysis occurs around day 26 of the cycle due to withdrawal of LH support (caused by high mid-luteal steroid feedback). The PDF key marks 'd' (low levels of estrogen and progesterone).
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 82
questions.hint: Luteolysis terminates steroidogenesis, precipitating menstrual bleeding.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: The progesterone levels rise to their highest point in female hormonal cycle

options.label: a
options.text: Between ovulation and beginning of menstruation

options.label: b
options.text: During follicular phase of ovarian cycle

options.label: d
options.text: When blood concentration of LH is at its highest point

questions.explanation: Progesterone peaks during the mid-luteal phase (days 21–22 of a 28-day cycle), which is situated between ovulation and the start of menstruation.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 82
questions.hint: Secreted predominantly by the mature corpus luteum in the second half of the cycle.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: Seven days after ovulation, pituitary secretion of luteinizing hormone (LH) decreases rapidly. What is the cause of this decrease in secretion?

options.label: a
options.text: The anterior pituitary gland becomes unresponsive to the stimulatory effect of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH)

options.label: b
options.text: Estrogen from the developing follicles exerts a feedback inhibition on the hypothalamus.

options.label: c
options.text: The rise in body temperature inhibits hypothalamic release of GnRH

options.label: d
options.text: Secretion of estrogen and progesterone by the corpus luteum suppresses hypothalamic secretion of GnRH and pituitary secretion of LH. FSH inhibits hypothalamic release of GnRH

questions.explanation: The PDF marked 'a'. Physiological note: At the mid-luteal peak (day 21 / 7 days post-ovulation), massive combined secretion of progesterone, estrogen, and inhibin by the corpus luteum exerts powerful negative feedback on both the hypothalamus and pituitary (option d describes this classical physiology). Marked 'a' in the exam key; flagged for review.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 82 (Female Hormonal System)
questions.hint: Marked 'a' in the PDF key regarding pituitary unresponsiveness.
questions.flag_reason: Textbook physiology emphasizes corpus luteum steroid negative feedback (d); PDF key marks option a.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: Why is milk produced only after delivery, not before?

options.label: a
options.text: Levels of luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone are too low during pregnancy to support milk production

options.label: b
options.text: High levels of progesterone and estrogen during pregnancy suppress milk production

options.label: c
options.text: The alveolar cells of the breast do not reach maturity until after delivery

options.label: d
options.text: High levels of oxytocin are required for milk production to begin, and oxytocin is not secreted until the baby stimulates the nipple

questions.explanation: During pregnancy, high circulating levels of placental estrogen and progesterone competitively block the lactogenic action of prolactin at breast alveolar receptors. The abrupt fall in estrogen and progesterone post-delivery releases this brake, initiating copious lactation.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 83 (Lactation)
questions.hint: High pregnancy sex steroids antagonize prolactin action on alveolar cells until placental expulsion.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: In order for the milk to flow from the nipple of the mother into the mouth of the nursing infant, which of the following must occur?

options.label: c
options.text: Oxytocin secretion from the posterior pituitary must take place

options.label: d
options.text: The baby's mouth develop a strong negative pressure over the nipple

questions.explanation: Active milk ejection requires the milk let-down reflex: suckling triggers neurosensory impulses to the paraventricular and supraoptic nuclei, causing posterior pituitary oxytocin release and contraction of myoepithelial cells.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 83
questions.hint: The neuroendocrine reflex releasing oxytocin to contract myoepithelial cells.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: After birth, the pressure in the pulmonary artery decreases greatly because:
questions.explanation: With the first breath, aeration of the lungs increases alveolar PO2, causing dramatic vasodilatation of pulmonary arterioles and decreasing pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) by more than 80%, sharply lowering pulmonary arterial pressure.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 84 (Neonatal Physiology)
questions.hint: Lung expansion and oxygenation relieve fetal pulmonary vasoconstriction.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: Which of the following could inhibit the initiation of labor?

options.label: c
options.text: Mechanically dilating and stimulating the cervix

questions.explanation: Progesterone maintains myometrial quiescence, hyperpolarizes myometrial smooth muscle cells, and suppresses oxytocin receptor expression and gap junction formation; administering progesterone prevents the onset of uterine contractions.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 83 (Parturition)
questions.hint: The 'pro-gestational' hormone that prevents uterine contractions.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: After menopause, hormone replacement therapy with estrogen-like compounds is effective in preventing the progression of osteoporosis. What is the mechanism of their protective effect?

options.label: a
options.text: They stimulate the activity of osteoblasts

options.label: b
options.text: They increase absorption of calcium from the gastrointestinal tract

options.label: c
options.text: They stimulate calcium reabsorption by the renal tubules

options.label: d
options.text: They stimulate parathyroid hormone (PTH) secretion by the parathyroid gland

questions.explanation: The PDF marked 'a) They stimulate the activity of osteoblasts'. NOTE: Clinically and physiologically, estrogen's primary mechanism in preventing bone loss is inhibiting osteoclastic bone resorption (via induction of osteoprotegerin [OPG] and suppressing RANKL/IL-6). However, estrogen also promotes osteoblast survival and collagen synthesis. Marked 'a' in the PDF key; flagged for review.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 80 & 82
questions.hint: Estrogen supports osteoblastic bone deposition and curbs osteoclasts.
questions.flag_reason: While estrogen primarily inhibits osteoclasts via OPG, PDF key marks osteoblast stimulation (a).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: A young woman is given daily injections of a substance beginning on the sixteenth day of her normal menstrual cycle and continuing for weeks. As long as the injections continue, she does not menstruate. The injected substance could be which of the following?
questions.explanation: CRITICAL DISCREPANCY: The PDF marks (c) 'An inhibitor of progesterone’s actions'. However, progesterone is REQUIRED to maintain the secretory endometrium! Blocking progesterone (e.g. with mifepristone) immediately triggers menstrual breakdown and uterine bleeding. To sustain the corpus luteum and PREVENT menstruation for weeks starting day 16, daily injections of hCG (option d) or exogenous progesterone are required! Flagged for human review.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 82 & 83
questions.hint: hCG rescues the corpus luteum to prevent menses; a progesterone inhibitor would trigger menses.
questions.flag_reason: Progesterone antagonists cause immediate menstruation; hCG prevents menstruation. PDF erroneously marked c.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.subtitle: Physiology MCQs
questions.question: A professional athlete in her mid-20s has not had a menstrual cycle for 5 years, although a bone density scan revealed normal skeletal mineralization. Which fact may explain these observations?

options.label: b
options.text: Her body pressure is higher than normal

options.label: c
options.text: Her plasma estrogen concentration is very low

options.label: d
options.text: She has been taking anabolic steroid supplements for 5 years

questions.explanation: CRITICAL DISCREPANCY: The PDF marks 'c) Her plasma estrogen concentration is very low'. However, hypoestrogenic athletic amenorrhea for 5 years leads to significant osteopenia/osteoporosis (female athlete triad). Normal bone mineralization despite 5 years of amenorrhea is characteristic of exogenous anabolic-androgenic steroid use (option d), which suppresses the HPO axis causing amenorrhea while powerfully stimulating osteoblasts and preserving bone mineral density. Flagged for review.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 81 & 82
questions.hint: Hypoestrogenemia causes bone loss; anabolic steroids cause amenorrhea while protecting bone density.
questions.flag_reason: Medical paradox: low estrogen for 5 yrs causes osteoporosis; anabolic steroids (d) preserve bone density. PDF marked c.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: Accumulation of lipofuscin in lysosomes is a marker of:
questions.explanation: Lipofuscin (tertiary lysosomes / residual bodies) accumulates in long-lived post-mitotic cells (neurons, cardiac myocytes) as an inevitable hallmark of cumulative cellular aging and free-radical autophagocytosis.
questions.source: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed., Chapter 1 & 2
questions.hint: The classic aging / wear-and-tear pigment in residual bodies.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: One of the following enzymes requires selenium for its adequate functioning.
questions.explanation: Glutathione peroxidase is a selenoprotein containing selenocysteine residues in its catalytic active site, which directly reduces toxic lipid hydroperoxides and H2O2.
questions.source: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd ed., Chapter 12 & 44 (Micronutrients)
questions.hint: Contains the 21st amino acid, selenocysteine.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: One of the following produces a free radical from L-arginine?
questions.explanation: Nitric oxide synthase (NOS) oxidizes L-arginine to L-citrulline and the free-radical signaling molecule nitric oxide (•NO) using NADPH and oxygen.
questions.source: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd ed., Chapter 48
questions.hint: Produces the potent vasodilator and reactive nitrogen radical •NO.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: Glutathione peroxidase activity requires which coenzyme?
questions.explanation: Glutathione peroxidase consumes reduced glutathione (GSH) to detoxify peroxides. Glutathione reductase then depends on NADPH (derived from the HMP shunt) to regenerate GSH from GSSG.
questions.source: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd ed., Chapter 20 (Pentose Phosphate Pathway)
questions.hint: NADPH from the pentose phosphate pathway fuels the glutathione redox cycle.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: Mutation in p53 gene promotes cancer mainly by:
questions.explanation: Loss-of-function TP53 mutations prevent transactivation of pro-apoptotic genes (such as BAX, PUMA, and NOXA), disabling apoptosis and allowing severely damaged, mutated cells to survive and proliferate.
questions.source: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed., Chapter 7
questions.hint: Mutated p53 fails to trigger programmed cell death in abnormal cells.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: HER2/neu amplification in breast cancer leads to:
questions.explanation: HER2 (ERBB2) is a receptor tyrosine kinase of the EGFR family. Gene amplification causes massive receptor overexpression, constitutive homodimerization/heterodimerization, and hyperactive downstream mitogenic MAPK and PI3K-Akt growth signaling.
questions.source: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed., Chapter 7 & 23
questions.hint: Overexpression of this tyrosine kinase receptor hyperactivates proliferative signaling pathways.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: Telomere shortening in somatic cells results in:
questions.explanation: Critically shortened telomeres trigger an irreversible DNA damage response recognized as double-strand breaks, locking normal somatic cells into permanent growth arrest (replicative cellular senescence).
questions.source: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed., Chapter 1
questions.hint: The Hayflick limit of irreversible replicative arrest.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: A 55-year-old man presents with unintentional weight loss, abdominal discomfort, and jaundice. On examination, he has hepatomegaly. Which of the following markers is most useful in this case?
questions.explanation: Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is the major oncofetal serum biomarker for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and non-seminomatous germ cell tumors of the testis.
questions.source: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed., Chapter 18 (Liver Tumors)
questions.hint: The quintessential diagnostic and surveillance tumor marker for hepatocellular carcinoma.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: Which reaction is a typical Phase I biotransformation?
questions.explanation: Phase I reactions introduce or expose a functional polar group (-OH, -NH2, -SH) via oxidation (predominantly hydroxylation by CYP450), reduction, or hydrolysis. Glucuronidation, sulfation, and methylation are Phase II conjugation reactions.
questions.source: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd ed., Chapter 47 (Xenobiotics)
questions.hint: Phase I oxidizes/hydroxylates; Phase II conjugates (glucuronidation, sulfation).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: A factory worker exposed to benzene develops toxic metabolites. Which enzyme family mediates the initial step?
questions.explanation: Benzene is metabolized in the liver by Cytochrome P450 (specifically CYP2E1) into benzene oxide, which subsequently generates toxic phenolic and quinone metabolites that induce bone marrow toxicity and leukemia.
questions.source: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed., Chapter 9 (Environmental Pathology)
questions.hint: Hepatic microsomal monooxygenase CYP2E1 mediates benzene bioactivation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: Downstream signalling of insulin receptor leading to GLUT-4 translocation is mediated by:
questions.explanation: Insulin binding autophosphorylates its receptor tyrosine kinase, recruiting IRS-1/2, activating Phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) and Protein Kinase B (Akt), which stimulates AS160 phosphorylation to trigger GLUT-4 vesicular translocation to the plasma membrane.
questions.source: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd ed., Chapter 42 (Hormone Action)
questions.hint: The metabolic arm of insulin signaling (contrasting with the mitogenic MAPK arm).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: First intracellular event after glucagon binding to its receptor is:
questions.explanation: Glucagon binds to a 7-transmembrane GPCR, triggering GDP-GTP exchange on the Gs-alpha subunit (G-protein activation). Activated Gs-alpha subsequently stimulates adenylyl cyclase to generate cAMP.
questions.source: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd ed., Chapter 42
questions.hint: Receptor conformational change directly triggers GDP-GTP exchange on the Gs alpha subunit.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: A 35-year-old woman presents with fatigue, cold intolerance, and dry skin. Her raised TSH levels will activate which second messenger pathway?
questions.explanation: The TSH receptor is a Gs-coupled GPCR. Binding activates adenylyl cyclase, elevating intracellular cyclic AMP, which activates Protein Kinase A (PKA) to stimulate thyroid follicular cell function and thyroglobulin endocytosis.
questions.source: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd ed., Chapter 41 & 42
questions.hint: TSH signals primarily through Gs → cAMP → PKA.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: A patient with Kallmann syndrome has anosmia and absent puberty. Which hypothalamic hormone deficiency is most responsible for this presentation?
questions.explanation: Kallmann syndrome is caused by failure of GnRH-secreting neurons and olfactory placode neurons to migrate together from the olfactory placode to the hypothalamus (KAL1/FGFR1 mutations), resulting in hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (absent puberty) and anosmia.
questions.source: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed., Chapter 24
questions.hint: Hypothalamic decapeptide governing LH and FSH secretion.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: A 45-year-old woman presents with symptoms of enlarged jaw, and deeper voice for last one year. Her rings no longer fit her. She also experienced headaches and vision problems. The raised hormone responsible for facial and voice changes exerts many of its effects through stimulation of which mediator?
questions.explanation: Acromegaly (from a GH-secreting somatotrope adenoma) produces soft-tissue and acral bone enlargement mediated primarily by hepatic synthesis and secretion of Insulin-like Growth Factor 1 (IGF-1).
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 76
questions.hint: The principal peripheral effector peptide mediating growth hormone's tissue actions.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: A 42-year-old woman with fatigue has low serum T4 and elevated TSH. Which enzyme in the thyroid gland catalyses both iodide oxidation and iodination of tyrosine residues in thyroglobulin?
questions.explanation: Thyroid peroxidase (TPO) is a membrane-bound apical hemoprotein that uses H2O2 to oxidize iodide (I– → I0/I+), iodinate tyrosyl residues on thyroglobulin (organification), and catalyze the coupling of iodotyrosines to form T3 and T4.
questions.source: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd ed., Chapter 41
questions.hint: The multifunctional apical enzyme targeted by antithyroid thionamides and Hashimoto autoantibodies.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: A 45-year-old female patient with goitre presented with heat intolerance, weight loss, and anxiety. The deranged hormone exerts its effects on molecular level by:
questions.explanation: Thyroid hormone (T3) diffuses into the nucleus and binds to thyroid hormone receptors (TRs, which heterodimerize with retinoid X receptors, RXR) bound to thyroid response elements (TRE) on chromatin to regulate gene transcription.
questions.source: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd ed., Chapter 41 & 42
questions.hint: Acts via zinc-finger nuclear transcription factor receptors bound to DNA.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: A 60-year-old man with chronic kidney disease presents with muscle cramps and tingling around the mouth. Labs reveal serum calcium of 7.2 mg/dL. One of the following mechanisms is responsible for hypocalcaemia in this patient.
questions.explanation: Loss of functional renal parenchyma in CKD reduces the activity of 1alpha-hydroxylase, impairing conversion of 25-(OH)D3 into active 1,25-(OH)2D3 (calcitriol), leading to diminished intestinal calcium absorption and hypocalcemia.
questions.source: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd ed., Chapter 44; Robbins 10th ed.
questions.hint: Loss of renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase impairs synthesis of the active vitamin D metabolite.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: A 50-year-old man presents with bone pain and kidney stones. Lab results revealed hypercalcemia, and reduced blood phosphate levels. This hypercalcemia is resulting from a raised hormone that leads to:
questions.explanation: Primary hyperparathyroidism causes hypercalcemia and hypophosphatemia. PTH binds osteoblasts, inducing RANKL expression, which binds RANK on osteoclast precursors to accelerate osteoclast maturation and bone resorption.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 80
questions.hint: PTH indirectly stimulates bone-resorbing cells to release calcium into blood.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: Which enzyme catalyses the rate-limiting step in adrenal steroid hormone synthesis?
questions.explanation: The conversion of cholesterol to pregnenolone by cholesterol desmolase (CYP11A1 / cholesterol side-chain cleavage enzyme), stimulated by ACTH/LH, is the rate-limiting committed step of steroidogenesis.
questions.source: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd ed., Chapter 41 (Adrenal Cortical Hormones)
questions.hint: The mitochondrial side-chain cleavage enzyme converting cholesterol to pregnenolone.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: A 3-day-old newborn presents with vomiting, dehydration, and hypotension. Examination reveals ambiguous genitalia. One of the following suggest 21-hydroxylase deficiency:

options.label: B
options.text: Decreased aldosterone and cortisol, increased androgens

options.label: D
options.text: Decreased cortisol, increased aldosterone and androgens

questions.explanation: 21-hydroxylase deficiency (the most common form of Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia) blocks synthesis of both aldosterone and cortisol, causing salt-wasting shock and diverting accumulated steroid precursors into adrenal androgen synthesis, virilizing female genitalia.
questions.source: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed., Chapter 24
questions.hint: Mineralocorticoid and glucocorticoid block with shunting into the androgenic pathway.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: Which glucose transporter is insulin-dependent in muscle and adipose tissue?
questions.explanation: GLUT-4 is the sole insulin-responsive facilitated glucose transporter, translocating from intracellular vesicles to the sarcolemma/plasma membrane of striated muscle and adipocytes upon insulin stimulation.
questions.source: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd ed., Chapter 19 & 42
questions.hint: The insulin-recruited transporter in striated muscle and adipose tissue.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: Pre-proinsulin is synthesized in which cellular organelle?
questions.explanation: Pre-proinsulin is translated by ribosomes docked on the rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER). The N-terminal signal sequence guides nascent pre-proinsulin into the RER cisternal lumen, where signal peptidase cleaves it to proinsulin.
questions.source: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd ed., Chapter 41 (Hormones of the Pancreas)
questions.hint: Ribosomes targeted to this organelle translate proteins destined for the secretory pathway.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: A 55-year-old man presents with difficulty in urination, weak stream, and increased nocturia. Examination reveals an enlarged, non-tender prostate. Which enzyme activity is most directly responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is driven by dihydrotestosterone (DHT), the potent androgen synthesized locally in prostatic stromal and epithelial cells by the enzyme 5alpha-reductase (type 2).
questions.source: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed., Chapter 21 (Prostate)
questions.hint: Converts testosterone into potent dihydrotestosterone (DHT); target of finasteride.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: A 27-year-old woman with infertility is found to have a mutation in the aromatase enzyme. Which of the following biochemical changes would most likely be seen in her ovarian steroid synthesis?

options.label: A
options.text: Accumulation of androgens with decreased oestrogen production

options.label: B
options.text: Increased conversion of cholesterol to pregnenolone

options.label: C
options.text: Increased synthesis of progesterone from pregnenolone

options.label: D
options.text: Accumulation of cortisol due to blocked oestrogen pathway

questions.explanation: Aromatase (CYP19A1) converts androstenedione to estrone and testosterone to estradiol. Congenital aromatase deficiency prevents estrogen synthesis, causing massive accumulation of substrate androgens (virilization, clitoromegaly, maternal virilization during pregnancy).
questions.source: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd ed., Chapter 41
questions.hint: Aromatase converts C19 androgens into C18 estrogens.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: A 32-year-old woman presents with recurrent early pregnancy losses. Laboratory evaluation suggests inadequate progesterone production during the luteal phase. Which of the following biochemical functions of progesterone explains her condition?

options.label: A
options.text: Increases uterine contractions and endometrial shedding

options.label: B
options.text: Maintains endometrium and suppresses uterine contractility

options.label: D
options.text: Enhances bone mineralization and LDL oxidation

questions.explanation: Progesterone transforms proliferative endometrium into a glandular secretory phase capable of sustaining blastocyst implantation and downregulates myometrial gap junctions to suppress contractility.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 82 & 83
questions.hint: Maintains the secretory decidua and calms the myometrium.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: A 45-year-old man with long-standing type 2 diabetes is on insulin therapy. To evaluate his residual pancreatic β-cell function, the physician orders a C-peptide test. Measurement of C-peptide is clinically important because it:

options.label: D
options.text: Is secreted in response to glucagon

questions.explanation: Connecting peptide (C-peptide) is cleaved from proinsulin in equimolar amounts to endogenous insulin during secretory granule maturation. Exogenous therapeutic insulin preparations contain no C-peptide, making it the ideal biomarker of endogenous beta-cell reserve.
questions.source: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd ed., Chapter 41
questions.hint: Secreted 1:1 with endogenous insulin and absent in pharmaceutical insulin.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.subtitle: Biochemistry MCQs
questions.question: A 30-year-old woman presents with weight loss despite increased appetite, palpitations, and heat intolerance. On examination, she has a diffuse goitre and exophthalmos. She is most likely suffering from:
questions.explanation: The clinical picture of hyperthyroidism, diffuse non-nodular goiter, and infiltrative ophthalmopathy (exophthalmos) is pathognomonic for Graves' disease (autoimmune thyroiditis with TSH-receptor stimulating antibodies).
questions.source: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed., Chapter 24 (Graves Disease)
questions.hint: Autoimmune hyperthyroidism with characteristic infiltrative ophthalmopathy.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A 60-year-old male came to medical OPD with history of nasal twang in voice. On examination, he had no taste sensation on the posterior one-third of the tongue and could not shrug his shoulder. MRI showed dural meningioma pressing upon nerves emerging through which of the following foramen?
questions.explanation: The jugular foramen transmits CN IX (loss of taste posterior 1/3 tongue), CN X (palatal paralysis with nasal twang in voice), and CN XI (paralysis of trapezius causing inability to shrug shoulder) — the classic Vernet's (jugular foramen) syndrome.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Cranial Foramina)
questions.hint: Transmits cranial nerves IX, X, and XI together with the internal jugular vein.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A patient suffers a head trauma in a road traffic accident and presents with an epidural hematoma. Imaging reveals the bleeding is likely from damage to the middle meningeal artery. Which one of the following skull landmarks is most likely to be fractured in this case?
questions.explanation: The anterior division of the middle meningeal artery grooves the inner table of the skull directly deep to the pterion, making it vulnerable to shearing in lateral craniocerebral trauma.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11
questions.hint: The cranial junction overlying the anterior ramus of the middle meningeal artery.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A young man got his scalp lacerated in a head-on collision during a car accident. He was taken to emergency as there was profuse bleeding from the gaped wound; few hours later, he developed a black eye. Which of the following layers of scalp has rich vascularization that leads to profuse bleeding?
questions.explanation: The second layer of the scalp (dense subcutaneous connective tissue) contains the primary arterial and venous networks. The dense fibrous septa hold severed vessels open, preventing retraction and vasospasm, leading to profuse arterial hemorrhage.
questions.source: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy, Vol. 3, Chapter 2 (Scalp)
questions.hint: Dense fibrous septa bind the blood vessels, preventing normal retraction after laceration.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A 1-year-old girl accidentally ingested bathroom cleaner and was brought to the emergency department. On examination, her pupils were dilated and she was unable to close her lips. Which of the following muscles may be paralyzed around the lips?
questions.explanation: The orbicularis oris muscle forms the circular sphincter around the mouth responsible for closing the lips and oral competence.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11
questions.hint: The circular muscle controlling closure of the oral fissure.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A 5-year-old female presented in emergency room with persistent pain and inability to close mouth for 6 hours. She gave history of yawning after which she was unable to close her mouth. X-ray showed bilateral dislocation of temporomandibular joint. Which one of the following muscle contractions leads to this condition?
questions.explanation: The lateral pterygoid is the only muscle of mastication that actively pulls the condyle and articular disc forward onto the articular eminence to open and protrude the jaw; overcontraction during yawning slides the condyle anterior to the eminence into the infratemporal fossa.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Muscles of Mastication)
questions.hint: The only masticatory muscle that depresses and protrudes the mandible.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A 45-year-old man presents to the emergency department with high-grade fever, severe pain, and swelling along the right side of his neck for the past 3 days. CT scan of the neck shows an abscess formation within the carotid sheath. Which of the following structures is most likely compressed?

options.label: a
options.text: Internal jugular vein and vagus nerve

options.label: b
options.text: Internal carotid artery and ansa cervicalis

options.label: c
options.text: Internal carotid artery and recurrent laryngeal nerve

options.label: d
options.text: Transverse cervical nerve and middle cervical ganglion

questions.explanation: The carotid sheath contains the common/internal carotid artery medially, internal jugular vein laterally, and vagus nerve (CN X) posteriorly between the vessels.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Carotid Sheath)
questions.hint: The major lateral venous channel and the tenth cranial nerve within the sheath.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following nerves runs alongside the superficial temporal artery?
questions.explanation: The auriculotemporal nerve (from CN V3) ascends over the root of the zygoma immediately posterior to the superficial temporal artery to supply sensation to the auricle and temple.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11
questions.hint: Sensory branch of CN V3 ascending anterior to the ear with this pulse-bearing artery.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A 35-year-old male arrives at the emergency department after a fistfight. He has a deep laceration just in front of his right ear with profuse pulsatile bleeding. Which one of the following arteries is most likely involved?
questions.explanation: The superficial temporal artery emerges from the upper border of the parotid gland and ascends in front of the tragus of the ear, where its superficial course renders it vulnerable to sharp preauricular trauma.
questions.source: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy, Vol. 3, Chapter 8
questions.hint: Terminal external carotid branch crossing the zygomatic arch immediately anterior to the tragus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A 22-year-old girl presented with swelling of left face with drooping corner of mouth and inability to raise her left eyebrow. Which one of the following structures is most likely affected?
questions.explanation: Inability to raise the ipsilateral eyebrow (paralysis of frontalis) combined with lower facial drooping indicates a LOWER motor neuron (LMN) facial nerve palsy (Bell's palsy pattern). Upper motor neuron lesions spare the forehead due to bilateral corticobulbar innervation.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Facial Nerve Lesions)
questions.hint: Forehead involvement is the cardinal differentiator confirming an LMN facial lesion.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A 52-year-old man presents two days after removal of an impacted right mandibular third molar with numbness of lower lip and chin. Which one of the following nerves was most likely injured?
questions.explanation: The inferior alveolar nerve runs in the mandibular canal directly below the roots of the impacted lower 3rd molar and gives off the mental nerve, which supplies sensation to the lower lip and chin.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Mandibular Nerve)
questions.hint: Traverses the mandibular canal and gives off the mental nerve.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A histological slide of a glandular structure shows mucous acini capped with serous demilunes. The specimen belongs to which gland?
questions.explanation: The submandibular salivary gland is characterized histologically by mixed seromucous units with mucous acini capped by crescentic serous demilunes.
questions.source: Wheater's Functional Histology, 6th ed., Chapter 13
questions.hint: Classic crescent-shaped serous demilunes cap mucous acini in this mixed gland.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: The submandibular duct opens into the oral cavity at which of the following sites?
questions.explanation: Wharton's duct opens onto the sublingual caruncle (papilla) on the floor of the mouth, immediately beside the base of the lingual frenulum.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11
questions.hint: The paired elevated papillae on either side of the base of the lingual frenulum.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A 48-year-old man after a head injury has medial strabismus of right eye. Which of the following ocular muscles is paralyzed in this injury?
questions.explanation: Paralysis of the lateral rectus (supplied by CN VI, abducens nerve) leaves the medial rectus (CN III) unopposed, pulling the eye medially (convergent/medial strabismus / esotropia).
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Cranial Nerve VI)
questions.hint: The abductor muscle of the eye; when paralyzed, the eye turns inward.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: The nasal field of the right eye is projected to which of the following parts of the right tract?

options.label: a
options.text: Left optic tract on its lateral side

options.label: b
options.text: Left optic tract on its medial side

options.label: c
options.text: Right optic tract on its medial side

options.label: d
options.text: Right optic tract on its lateral side

questions.explanation: Light from the right nasal visual field strikes the right temporal hemiretina. Fibers from the temporal hemiretina remain uncrossed and pass through the lateral aspect of the chiasm into the ipsilateral (right) optic tract. In the optic tract, uncrossed fibers occupy a specific position. Marked 'c' in the PDF key.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 52
questions.hint: Fibers from the temporal retina viewing the nasal field remain in the ipsilateral optic tract.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Damage to which retinal layer would affect rod cells responsible for perception of light?
questions.explanation: The cell bodies and nuclei of the rod and cone photoreceptors are situated within the outer nuclear layer (ONL) of the retina.
questions.source: Wheater's Functional Histology, 6th ed., Chapter 21
questions.hint: Contains the nucleated somas of the photoreceptor cells.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A 10-year-old child with chronic otitis media and perforated tympanic membrane presents with hearing loss. Which of the following nerves is most likely affected?
questions.explanation: The chorda tympani branch of CN VII crosses the medial surface of the tympanic membrane between the handle of the malleus and incus, making it directly vulnerable to tympanic perforations and chronic suppurative otitis media.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Middle Ear)
questions.hint: Crosses directly across the upper portion of the tympanic membrane.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: The external ear develops from which embryological arches?
questions.explanation: The auricle (pinna) develops from six mesenchymal proliferations (auricular hillocks of His): three from the first pharyngeal arch and three from the second pharyngeal arch surrounding the first cleft.
questions.source: Langman's Medical Embryology, 14th ed., Chapter 19
questions.hint: The 6 auricular hillocks of His derive equally from arches 1 and 2.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A 30-year-old man undergoes thyroid surgery and develops difficulty swallowing. Which nerve supplying the pharyngeal constrictor muscles is most likely injured?
questions.explanation: All three pharyngeal constrictor muscles (superior, middle, and inferior) are innervated by motor branches of the vagus nerve (CN X via pharyngeal plexus and external laryngeal nerve).
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Pharynx)
questions.hint: Provides motor fibers to all pharyngeal constrictors via the pharyngeal plexus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A 64-year-old man with ulcers on the lateral edge of the anterior tongue has inability to protrude the tongue. Which of the following muscles is affected?
questions.explanation: The genioglossus muscle originates from the superior mental spine of the mandible and inserts into the tongue dorsum; bilateral contraction protrudes the tongue.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11
questions.hint: The primary muscle protruding the tongue.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: The posterior one-third of the tongue is derived from which pharyngeal arch?
questions.explanation: The hypobranchial eminence (copula) overgrows the second arch, so the mucosa of the posterior third of the tongue is derived embryologically from the third pharyngeal arch.
questions.source: Langman's Medical Embryology, 14th ed., Chapter 17
questions.hint: The arch supplied by CN IX.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A person with trauma to tongue has injury to the dorsal surface of anterior two-thirds. Which papilla type is most abundant and likely injured?
questions.explanation: Filiform papillae are the most abundant and numerous papillae covering the entire dorsal surface of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
questions.source: Wheater's Functional Histology, 6th ed., Chapter 13
questions.hint: Small, conical, non-gustatory papillae covering the vast majority of the tongue dorsum.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: After maxillary molar extraction, a patient develops purulent nasal discharge. The tooth root has entered the maxillary sinus. Drainage of this sinus occurs through which nasal meatus?
questions.explanation: The maxillary sinus drains through its natural ostium high on its medial wall into the middle meatus (via the lower portion of the hiatus semilunaris).
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Maxillary Sinus)
questions.hint: Drains into the hiatus semilunaris beneath the middle concha.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Epistaxis from Kiesselbach’s area mainly involves which artery?
questions.explanation: Kiesselbach's plexus is an anastomotic network of four arteries: sphenopalatine, anterior ethmoidal, greater palatine, and superior labial. The sphenopalatine artery is the chief arterial contributor.
questions.source: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 10th ed., Chapter 11 (Little's Area)
questions.hint: The terminal branch of the maxillary artery feeding the plexus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: During thyroid surgery, ligation of the inferior thyroid artery may injure which nerve?
questions.explanation: The recurrent laryngeal nerve ascends in the tracheoesophageal groove, intimately crossing or intertwining with terminal branches of the inferior thyroid artery near the inferior pole of the thyroid gland.
questions.source: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 27th ed., Chapter 48
questions.hint: Must be ligated well away from the gland to protect this nerve.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: In elderly people, which laryngeal cartilage is most prone to fracture?
questions.explanation: The thyroid cartilage is hyaline cartilage that undergoes progressive endochondral ossification and calcification with advancing age, becoming rigid and brittle, predisposing it to fracture during blunt cervical trauma.
questions.source: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy, Vol. 3, Chapter 14 (Larynx)
questions.hint: Large hyaline cartilage forming the 'Adam's apple' that ossifies in late adulthood.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A midline neck swelling just above thyroid cartilage that moves on swallowing is most likely:
questions.explanation: Thyroglossal duct cysts occur in the midline of the neck (often infrahyoid / above thyroid cartilage) and move upward during swallowing and tongue protrusion.
questions.source: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 27th ed., Chapter 48
questions.hint: Midline congenital cyst moving characteristically with swallowing and tongue protrusion.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.question: A patient with uncorrected myopia complains of blurred distant vision. Which change in the ocular part is primarily responsible?

options.label: a
options.text: Elongated eyeball resulting in image formation anterior to the retina

options.label: b
options.text: Flattened cornea causing reduced converging power

options.label: c
options.text: Lens sclerosis leading to loss of elasticity

options.label: d
options.text: Short axial length of the eyeball

questions.explanation: In axial myopia (nearsightedness), the anteroposterior diameter of the eyeball is abnormally long, causing parallel rays from distant objects to converge to a focal point in front of (anterior to) the retina.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 50 (Refractive Errors)
questions.hint: Excessive axial length focuses light in front of the retina.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.question: A patient with vitamin A deficiency has night blindness. What is the most likely underlying mechanism?

options.label: c
options.text: Failure of aqueous humor to support retinal metabolism

options.label: d
options.text: Reduced rhodopsin formation in rod cells

questions.explanation: Vitamin A (all-trans-retinol) is the direct precursor to 11-cis-retinal, the chromophore of rhodopsin. Deficiency causes failure of rhodopsin resynthesis in rods, impairing scotopic night vision (nyctalopia).
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 50
questions.hint: 11-cis-retinal is essential to regenerate the rod visual pigment rhodopsin.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.question: When light hits a rod photoreceptor, which event initiates signal transduction?

options.label: a
options.text: Activation of retinal ganglion cells by glutamate release

options.label: b
options.text: Closure of cGMP-gated Na⁺ channels causing hyperpolarization

options.label: c
options.text: Depolarization due to influx of Ca²⁺

options.label: d
options.text: Opening of Na⁺ channels by cGMP

questions.explanation: Light photoisomerizes 11-cis-retinal to all-trans-retinal, activating transducin and phosphodiesterase, which degrades cGMP. Reduced cGMP closes outer segment cation channels, causing hyperpolarization.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 50
questions.hint: Decreased cGMP leads to closure of sodium channels and membrane hyperpolarization.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.question: A 16-year-old girl underwent surgery for resection of a pituitary tumor. After surgery, she experienced blindness in the temporal fields of both eyes. Which of the following is affected?
questions.explanation: The optic chiasm lies directly superior to the sella turcica and pituitary fossa; surgical trauma or tumor mass effect to the crossing nasal fibers causes bitemporal hemianopia.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 52
questions.hint: The decussation of optic nerve fibers sitting right above the pituitary.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.question: A patient with red-green color blindness lacks which of the following?

options.label: c
options.text: Green and red cone photopigment opsins

questions.explanation: Red-green color blindness (protanopia/deuteranopia) is an X-linked recessive disorder resulting from absence or mutation of either the L-cone (red) or M-cone (green) photopigment opsin genes.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 50 (Color Vision)
questions.hint: Inability to distinguish red and green stems from defects in red or green cone opsin proteins.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Which adhesion molecules are primarily reduced during metastasis, allowing tumor cells to detach from the primary site?
questions.explanation: E-cadherin maintains homotypic calcium-dependent intercellular junctions between epithelial cells. Downregulation or loss of E-cadherin is the hallmark of epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), enabling carcinoma detachment and invasion.
questions.source: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed., Chapter 7 (Invasion and Metastasis)
questions.hint: Calcium-dependent intercellular adherens junction proteins.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: The MYC oncogene primarily promotes cancer by which of the following phenomena?
questions.explanation: MYC is a master basic helix-loop-helix leucine zipper transcription factor that binds E-box sequences, driving widespread transcription of cyclins, CDKs, rRNA, and metabolic genes promoting cell proliferation.
questions.source: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed., Chapter 7 (Oncogenes)
questions.hint: Functions as a nuclear transcription factor accelerating the cell cycle.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Superoxide anion (O₂•–) is mainly generated during which of the following processes?
questions.explanation: During mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, approximately 1–2% of electrons traveling through Complexes I and III of the electron transport chain prematurely leak directly to O2, generating superoxide radicals (O2•–).
questions.source: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd ed., Chapter 12 (Biological Oxidation)
questions.hint: Mitochondrial electron transport chain leak during aerobic respiration.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Which repair mechanism helps cells combat protein damage caused by wear and tear?
questions.explanation: Misfolded, oxidatively damaged, or senescent intracellular proteins are covalently tagged with ubiquitin and targeted to the 26S proteasome for degradation into reusable oligopeptides.
questions.source: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd ed., Chapter 4 & 49
questions.hint: The ubiquitin-proteasome system clears damaged cellular proteins.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: A patient undergoing treatment with sulfonamide drugs develops hemolytic anemia. Laboratory tests show decreased reduced glutathione levels in red blood cells. Which cofactor is most likely deficient in this case?
questions.explanation: In Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, erythrocyte generation of NADPH via the HMP shunt is impaired. Without NADPH, glutathione reductase cannot regenerate reduced glutathione (GSH), rendering RBCs susceptible to oxidant stress from sulfonamides and causing acute intravascular hemolysis.
questions.source: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd ed., Chapter 20 (Pentose Phosphate Pathway)
questions.hint: The essential reducing cofactor produced by G6PD in erythrocytes.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: A 50-year-old man on long-term antiepileptic therapy develops increased metabolism of other co-administered drugs. The physician suspects induction of liver enzymes. Which enzyme system is most likely induced in this patient?
questions.explanation: Antiepileptic medications (such as carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital) are potent inducers of hepatic Cytochrome P450 enzymes (e.g. CYP3A4), accelerating Phase I oxidative metabolism of co-administered drugs.
questions.source: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd ed., Chapter 47 (Xenobiotics)
questions.hint: The inducible microsomal monooxygenase enzyme superfamily.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Which of the following is a Phase I reaction in xenobiotic metabolism?
questions.explanation: Phase I reactions consist of oxidation, reduction, and hydrolysis reactions. Acetylation, glucuronidation, and sulfation are Phase II conjugation reactions.
questions.source: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd ed., Chapter 47
questions.hint: Oxidation is the quintessential Phase I reaction introducing reactive polar handles.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Epinephrine and norepinephrine belong to which class of hormones?
questions.explanation: Epinephrine and norepinephrine are catecholamines, synthesized through enzymatic decarboxylation and hydroxylation of the aromatic amino acid L-tyrosine.
questions.source: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd ed., Chapter 41
questions.hint: Derived from the aromatic amino acid tyrosine.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Thyroid hormones act through which of the following receptors?
questions.explanation: Thyroid hormones (T3/T4) bind directly to intracellular nuclear receptors (TR-alpha and TR-beta) that act as ligand-activated transcription factors on chromatin.
questions.source: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd ed., Chapter 41 & 42
questions.hint: Intracellular receptors that bind DNA response elements directly.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: A 25-year-old woman presents with amenorrhea and infertility. Lab results reveal low FSH and LH levels. MRI shows a lesion in the hypothalamus impairing secretion of a releasing hormone. Which hypothalamic hormone is most likely deficient?
questions.explanation: Hypothalamic GnRH stimulates the synthesis and pulsatile secretion of LH and FSH from anterior pituitary gonadotrophs. Deficiency leads to hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, amenorrhea, and anovulatory infertility.
questions.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., Chapter 82
questions.hint: The hypothalamic releasing factor that regulates pituitary gonadotrophs.
